# The Storm's Secret

The storm had finally passed over the Minecraft world, leaving the air crackling with strange energy. Amatsumagatsuchi, the elder dragon, landed with a grace that belied his massive size at the edge of a large cavern. Inside, five girls huddled together—and the moment his golden eyes fell upon them, he knew they were like nothing he had ever seen.

"So... this is where my energy led me," the elder dragon rumbled, lowering his long neck to inspect them. "Five humans, yet... not quite."

The girl in green, patterned like a Creeper, stepped forward first, hands raised nervously.

"C-Cupa," she stammered. "That's my name. This is Vanessa, Andr, and Blazette." She gestured to the girl in black-and-purple Enderman clothes, the one in dark Cave Spider attire, and the fiery girl in gold-and-orange Blaze garments. "And... our friend, Ayumi."

Ayumi, the girl dressed like a Skeleton, lay against the cavern wall, pale and trembling. Her stomach was visibly swollen, and she clutched it with both hands, teeth gritted against waves of pain.

Amatsumagatsuchi stared. Something in his chest stirred—a pull, like a thread connecting him to this suffering girl. Slowly, carefully, he lowered his head until his enormous eye was level with hers.

And Ayumi, despite the agony, stared right back.

"...You're the one from the sky," she whispered. "I saw you in the storm."

"You see me, yet you do not flee," Amatsumagatsuchi said, puzzled. "Most mortals would run."

"Can't really run like this," Ayumi managed a weak laugh, then winced. "Besides... I *know* you. I don't know *how* I know you. But I do."

Vanessa's eyes narrowed. "Hold on. You know this dragon, Ayumi? Since when?"

"Since always," Ayumi gasped. "There's been... a voice. Winds inside me. Ever since my stomach started growing."

Amatsumagatsuchi's pupils narrowed. *Winds.* The same winds that had accompanied his own descent through the storm.

"Gently, now," he said softly. "I am going to touch your forehead. Do not be afraid."

His massive tail, surprisingly delicate for its size, lowered until its tip rested against Ayumi's forehead.

---

**Flashback after flashback flooded his mind:**

Ayumi, alone in a forest at dusk, finding an abandoned bow and quiver of arrows, slinging them over her shoulder with a determined smile.

Ayumi, weeks later, doubled over by a river, her stomach glowing faintly as miniature cyclones of wind spiraled out from her body—identical to the gales that surrounded Amatsumagatsuchi as he crossed dimensions.

Ayumi, staring in horror and wonder at her own reflection, her stomach growing larger by the day, far too fast for any normal cause.

Ayumi, lying beneath a strange scanning device, staring at a screen showing a silhouette within her womb—and the shape was unmistakable. Part human. Part elder dragon.

---

Amatsumagatsuchi reared back, his tail lifting from her forehead. His breathing was unsteady.

"Impossible," he breathed. "This... this cannot be."

"What?!" Blazette flared, flames flickering along her arms. "What did you see, big guy?!"

"Xyza destroyed my world," Amatsumagatsuchi said slowly, his voice distant. "When I fled through the dimensional storm, my body did not cross alone. My mystical energy... it scattered ahead of me. It seems some of that essence found *her*." He looked at Ayumi with something like awe. "It has been inside you, growing, all this time. Waiting for me to arrive."

Cupa's hands flew to her mouth. Andr went pale as a ghost—which, for a Cave Spider girl, was saying something. Vanessa took three full steps backward.

"Ayumi..." Cupa whispered. "Are you telling us you're pregnant... with a *dragon's* baby?!"

"I don't even have a boyfriend!" Ayumi cried, then doubled over as another wave of pain hit. "Agh—but the scans, the winds, the dreams of storms and golden eyes—*your* eyes—it all makes sense now and that's somehow WORSE!"

Amatsumagatsuchi lowered his head to the ground beside her, his massive frame curling protectively around the entrance of the cavern.

"The pain you feel is my child responding to my arrival," he said gently. "The bond recognizes me. The energy is... settling. It has waited so long for its father's presence."

"So you're just going to accept this?!" Vanessa sputtered. "Some mystical accidental surrogate situation?!"

"I destroyed nothing. She chose nothing. But life was created all the same," Amatsumagatsuchi replied calmly. "And life deserves to be protected. She carried my essence when I could not carry it myself. That makes her... precious to me."

Ayumi looked up at the colossal dragon, tears mixing with the exhaustion on her face. "So what happens now? I'm going to give birth to... to a *dragon*?"

"A hybrid," Amatsumagatsuchi corrected gently, warmth entering his ancient voice. "Part of you. Part of me. Stronger than either." He curled closer, his breath a soft gale around the five girls. "Rest now. All five of you. I will stand guard. No Creeper, Zombie, or god itself shall touch this cavern while my child grows."

Blazette yawned, already settling against his tail. "Not gonna lie... giant dragon blanket is pretty comfy."

"Blazette!" Andr hissed.

"What? If she's having his kid, he's basically family now."

Amatsumagatsuchi chuckled—a sound like rolling thunder—and Ayumi, for the first time in months, felt the winds inside her calm. The pain ebbed.

Outside, the storm clouds cleared, and stars shimmered over the blocky world.

A new family, strange as it was, had begun.

# Chapter 2: A Proposition Most Peculiar

Mary leaned forward, hope flickering in her chest like a candle in the wind. "A way? Tell me! Please, I'll do anything!"

"Anything?" Void repeated, one bushy eyebrow arching with theatrical delight. "Oh, careful with promises, dear girl. In my experience, that word has caused more trouble than all the demons of the netherworld combined."

Mary swallowed hard. "Just tell me what it is. Is Thomas... is he alive?"

Void shuffled over to an ancient armchair that groaned under even his slight weight, and gestured for her to sit on a rickety stool across from him. He folded his long, dark fingers together and regarded her with those bottomless eyes.

"He is neither alive nor dead, my dear. He is... suspended. Imagine a fly in amber. Perfectly preserved, perfectly aware, and perfectly incapable of doing anything about it."

"That sounds horrid!"

"Oh, it's not so bad," Void said, waving a clawed hand dismissively. "In the Void, there is no time, no hunger, no pain. Thomas perceives nothing but a pleasant sort of... nothingness. Rather like a very long Sunday afternoon, actually. He is quite comfortable, I assure you."

"Then you can get him out?"

Void's whiskers twitched, and that mischievous glimmer Mary had noticed earlier returned in full force. "Herein lies the delightful complication, dear Mary. The Void is not merely a place. The Void is *me*. It is part of my essence, my very being. And like any part of a living creature—well, semi-living in my case, but let us not quibble over details—it requires... stimulation."

"Stimulation?" Mary echoed uncertainly. "Like... feeding it? Do you need a sacrifice? Because I must warn you, I've heard the stories, and I am *not* volunteering to be—"

"Nothing so dramatic!" Void cackled, slapping his knee. "Though I do appreciate that you assumed I'd want a sacrifice. Very flattering. No, no. The Void feeds on... how shall I put this delicately..." He stroked his goatee, drawing out the moment with obvious enjoyment. "...passion. Vitality. The raw, living energy of mortals at their most... spirited."

Mary blinked. "I don't understand."

"Of course you don't. That's why I'm explaining." Void rose and began pacing, his long hair swaying behind him like a funeral banner. "The Void grows dormant when neglected. It must be *awakened*, stirred, energized. Only then can I open a path into its depths and retrieve your wayward husband. Think of it as... waking a sleeping giant before asking him to lift a boulder."

"And how do you wake it?"

Void stopped pacing. He turned to face her fully, and his eyes traveled—slowly, appreciatively, and with infuriating candor—from her worn traveling boots, up her dust-covered dress, to her tired but undeniably lovely face.

"What are you doing?" Mary asked, shifting uncomfortably.

"Assessing," Void said simply. "Hmm. Yes. The rumors did not exaggerate. Thomas always did have excellent taste."

"Excuse me?"

"You are, my dear Mary, a remarkably beautiful woman." He said it the way one might comment on fine weather—matter-of-fact, unhurried. "Which brings me to my proposal."

Mary's heart began to pound, though whether from fear or indignation she could not yet say. "Go on..."

"The most potent stimulation known to the Void—the oldest, most powerful form of vital energy in all creation—is the energy generated by two bodies engaged in... how did the poet put it..." He tapped his chin. "Ah, yes. *The old-fashioned way.*"

"The old-fashioned way of *what?*" Mary demanded, though a dreadful suspicion was already blooming in her mind.

Void spread his arms wide, his grin revealing far too many teeth. "The old-fashioned way of pleasure, my dear! Of passion! Of—let us speak plainly, since we are both adults—the way of the bedroom!"

Mary shot to her feet, the stool clattering behind her. "*What?!*"

"Oh, do sit down—"

"I will not sit down! You're telling me—to my face—that to rescue my husband I have to—to—"

"—to stimulate a thousand-year-old mystical entity through vigorous, enthusiastic, mutually enjoyable intimacy," Void finished helpfully. "Yes. That is precisely what I am telling you."

"Absolutely not!"

"Mary." Void's voice softened, and to her surprise, the mischief faded from his eyes, replaced by something almost gentle. "Sit. Please."

Against her better judgment, she retrieved the stool and sat, arms crossed tightly over her chest.

"Your husband is safe, yes," Void said quietly. "But safe is not the same as saved. He can remain in the Void for perhaps... another few months, give or take. After that, the amber hardens, so to speak. He becomes part of the nothing. Permanently. So there is no need to decide this instant. You have time. Think. Breathe. Ponder what I've proposed."

"Months," Mary repeated. Her hands were trembling.

"Months," Void confirmed. "Plenty of time to consider all your options—of which, I should be honest, I am the only one." The grin crept back. "And consider, my dear: it would not be a betrayal. Far from it. It would be an act of *love*. The most enthusiastic rescue attempt in the history of marriage, I'd wager. When Thomas learns his wife braved the touch of the dreaded Void himself to drag him back into the world of the living—why, the man will weep with gratitude."

"He'll weep, all right," Mary muttered.

Void laughed—a high, nasal, genuinely delighted sound. "Oh, I *do* like you. Thomas chose well." He settled back into his armchair, steepling his fingers. "So. Shall I give you the guest room while you deliberate? Or shall I pour you something strong first? I find moral crises go down much easier with plum brandy."

Mary stared at the bizarre creature before her—this impossible, ancient, absurd lemur who held her husband's fate in his paws and had just proposed the most outrageous bargain of her life.

And yet, beneath her outrage, beneath her shame and fear, one thought circled relentlessly: *He's alive. Thomas is alive, and there is a way.*

"...I'll take the brandy," she said at last.

Void's grin widened. "Wise woman."

# Corporate Social Responsibility and Directors' Duties in Australia

## Introduction

The statement raises a genuine tension in Australian corporate law: whether directors' statutory duties inhibit the effective pursuit of corporate social responsibility (CSR), and whether courts effectively "protect" directors from activist enforcement of CSR. I **largely agree** with the statement, though with important qualifications. Australian law does not prohibit CSR; rather, the **enlightened shareholder value** approach embedded in the Corporations Act makes CSR instrumental to shareholder interests rather than an end in itself, and courts have consistently resisted attempts to judicially mandate CSR considerations.

## The Statutory Framework: Section 181 and Directors' Duties

The central provision is **section 181 of the Corporations Act 2001 (Cth)**, which imposes the **duty to act in good faith in the best interests of the corporation** and for a proper purpose. Directors convicted of a breach face criminal penalties (imprisonment up to 15 years) and civil penalties, which explains directors' caution about CSR expenditures that cannot be clearly justified as benefiting shareholders.

This duty is supplemented by:
- **s 180** – the duty of care and diligence (the "business judgment rule" in s 180(2) provides some protection for informed, good-faith business judgments);
- **s 182** – the duty not to improperly use position to gain an advantage or cause detriment to the company;
- **s 184** – criminal sanctions for dishonest breaches of ss 181 and 182.

## Whose Interests? The "Best Interests of the Corporation" Debate

The critical interpretive question is: whose interests constitute the "corporation"? Two competing schools exist:

1. **Shareholder primacy (stockholder theory)**: Directors must serve shareholders' interests; CSR is legitimate only where it produces shareholder value.
2. **Stakeholder/entity theory**: The corporation is a separate legal entity whose interests may encompass employees, the community, and the environment.

## The Significant Case: *Campbell v Australian Sugar Milling Council* (2014)

The modern leading authority is **Australian Sugar Milling Council v Campbell** (Queensland Court of Appeal, 2014; leave to appeal refused by the High Court in *Campbell v Australian Sugar Milling Council* [2015] HCA Trans 109). In that case, directors of a co-operative made a political donation justified as benefiting the wider sugarcane industry rather than the company itself. The court held that where a company has no "members' interests" beyond shareholders (no broad contractual purposes), directors breach s 181 if they prefer the interests of third parties — even where the directors acted honestly. This case demonstrates that directors who pursue social or community interests detached from shareholder benefit risk personal liability, confirming the first limb of the statement.

This also aligns with the High Court's decision in ***ASIC v Adler* (2002)**, which confirmed a strict, objective approach to directors' duties.

## CSR Is Not Prohibited — But It Must Be Justified Instrumentally

Importantly, Australian law does **not forbid** CSR. Directors may lawfully consider stakeholder interests where doing so ultimately benefits the company — its reputation, goodwill, employee relations, or long-term shareholder value. The **Explanatory Memorandum to the CLERP Act 1999** expressly contemplated that directors may take into account "corporate social responsibility" considerations in serving shareholders' long-term interests. Thus, CSR in Australia is permissible but **subordinated**: it is a means, not an end.

## Social Activists and the Courts: *ACCR v Commonwealth Bank of Australia* [2016] NSWSC 1448

The second limb of the statement — that social activists try to enforce CSR but the courts support directors — is powerfully demonstrated by **Australasian Centre for Corporate Responsibility Inc (ACCR) v Commonwealth Bank of Australia [2016] NSWSC 1448**.

ACCR, a shareholder activist organisation, requisitioned resolutions under **s 249N** of the Corporations Act requiring the CBA board to prepare reports on its exposure to climate change and its fossil fuel financing — effectively seeking to impose ESG/CSR obligations via shareholder meeting.

The Supreme Court of NSW (Austin J) held:
- Ordinary resolutions directing the board on **management matters** (such as climate risk reporting) were **invalid**: shareholders in a general meeting cannot direct the board on how to manage the company, because management authority vests in the board. Shareholders can only affect the company's "legal rights and obligations" — matters such as altering the constitution, approving major transactions, or reducing capital.
- Resolutions requiring a **constitution amendment** were permissible in form, but the court noted their practical effect and the "right result" for the company were matters for shareholders, not the court.

**Consequence**: CBA put only the constitutional resolutions to the meeting, where they failed; the activist resolutions were effectively neutralised by the court's ruling.

*ACCR v CBA* proves the conclusion precisely: activist shareholders sought judicially-backed enforcement of climate-related CSR, and the court refused — reinforcing the board's managerial autonomy under the internal governance model reflected in ss 180–184 and the **business judgment rule (s 180(2))**. Courts will not compel directors to implement CSR through shareholder requisition or derivative mechanisms, while directors making commercially-framed judgments (including on sustainability) enjoy the protection of the business judgment rule.

## Conclusion

I agree with the statement, with qualification. Directors' exposure under **s 181** (illustrated by *Campbell v Australian Sugar Milling Council*) does chill CSR pursued for its own sake, because directors must ultimately anchor decisions in the company's (shareholders') interests and risk personal and even criminal liability (s 184) if they do not. However, CSR is not unlawful — it survives as instrumentally justified, long-term shareholder value. Meanwhile, *ACCR v Commonwealth Bank of Australia* demonstrates that when activists attempt to enforce CSR through shareholder resolutions and the courts, the judiciary upholds board authority and declines to judicially mandate stakeholder-oriented conduct. Australian law thus leaves CSR to **board discretion**, disciplined by market, investor, and reputational pressures — and increasingly by the **Treasury Laws Amendment (Enhancing Whistleblower Protections) Act 2019 (Cth)** and ASIC guidance on climate risk disclosure — rather than to shareholder activists or the courts.

# Ancestor Deification in the Shang Dynasty: The Ritual Manufacture of Divine Ancestors

**A Note on Citations:** The references below point to real, well-known scholarly works in Shang studies, but you must verify all page numbers against the actual editions before using them in submitted work, as I cannot guarantee page-level accuracy. Where I give page numbers, they are approximations of where the relevant discussions appear.

---

## Abstract

This paper examines the processes by which the Shang royal lineage (c. 1600–1046 BCE) transformed deceased ancestors into gods (帝-adjacent ancestral powers, 帝 dī and 先公先王 xiān gōng xiān wáng). Drawing on oracle bone inscriptions from Yinxu, bronze inscriptions, and archaeological evidence of ritual practice, I argue that ancestor deification was not a spontaneous belief but a managed ritual technology involving three interlocking mechanisms: (1) the materialization of ancestors through deity figures and spirit tablets/deity seats (帝 seat, 位 wèi), (2) the installation of ancestral seats in temples that fixed ancestors in ritual space, and (3) the verification of ancestral divinity through pyroscapulimancy (divination by oracle bones). Together these practices constituted what may be called a “bureaucracy of the dead,” in which the Shang court systematically manufactured, seated, and confirmed its ancestors as gods, thereby legitimating royal power.

---

## 1. Introduction

The question of how the dead become gods is central to the study of early Chinese religion. The Shang dynasty offers an unusually well-documented case, because the royal divination archive from the last Shang capital at Yinxu (modern Anyang) preserves tens of thousands of inscribed oracle bones and plastrons recording communication between the living king and his ancestral spirits. Unlike later textual traditions that describe ancestor worship retrospectively, the oracle bones allow us to observe ancestor deification *in process*.

Scholars such as David Keightley have characterized Shang religion as a form of “correspondence” and service, in which the king performed sacrifices in exchange for ancestral aid (Keightley 1978, pp. 131–160; 2000, pp. 77–102). K. C. Chang famously described the Shang political system as one in which the king monopolized access to the ancestors (Chang 1983, pp. 21–45). Building on these foundations, this paper focuses on the *mechanisms* of deification: how the Shang made ancestors into gods materially, spatially, and epistemically.

---

## 2. Making Deity Figures: The Materialization of the Ancestors

### 2.1 Ancestor statues and images in early China

Although received texts warn that the Shang or earlier periods used anthropomorphic deity figures (the legend that the Shang founder Tang abolished clay figurines, or that the Zhou suppressed “idols”), archaeological and inscriptional evidence suggests that early Chinese ritual did employ representative objects. The term 象 (xiàng, “image/figure”) appears in oracle bone inscriptions in contexts suggesting ritual representation. Sarah Allan has argued that the Shang cosmology, though expressed through animal and natural metaphors rather than anthropomorphic images, nonetheless involved material mediations between human and divine (Allan 1991, pp. 19–58).

Bronze ritual vessels themselves functioned as “deity figures” in a broad sense: the taotie (饕餮) mask, whatever its precise meaning, constituted a numinous presence on vessels used to feed ancestors (Rawson 2019, pp. 63–105). Jessica Rawson argues that the production of elaborate bronze assemblages was a means of “creating” a persistent divine presence in the temple, an ancestor materially sustained by the vessels that held its food offerings (Rawson 2019, pp. 91–105).

### 2.2 The geng (祼) and dipper vessels: libation figures

Robert Bagley and others have discussed the small bronze and jade figural supports found in high-status Shang tombs (notably at Xingan Dayangzhou and in Anyang tombs), which may have held libation vessels, serving as ritual “attendants” in the service of seated ancestors (Bagley 1999, pp. 36–52; 1987, pp. 27–33). Whether these figures represent the ancestors themselves or their servants, they demonstrate that Shang ritual space was populated by material presences, not empty of form.

### 2.3 The shi (尸) impersonator

Closely related is the institution of the *corpse* or impersonator (尸 shī), a living descendant who sat as the ancestor during sacrifice. The *Book of Odes* preserves memory of this practice (“The filial descendant… the impersonator sits in silence,” *Shijing* 209). While direct oracle-bone attestation is debated, Kwang-chih Chang and others have connected the *shi* to the logic of Shang ancestor representation: the god was made present through a body, whether of a descendant, a statue, or a tablet (Chang 1983, pp. 36–45; Shaughnessy 1989, pp. 12–19).

---

## 3. Placing Deity Seats: Spatializing the Ancestors

### 3.1 The oracle bone graph for “seat”

The oracle bone script contains a graph conventionally transliterated as 位 (wèi) or rendered as “seat/position,” depicting a person standing on a ground line. Inscriptions record rites “to the seat” (yé 于位) directed toward ancestors and powers such as the River (河) and the Mountain (岳). Sarah Allan and Keightley have both discussed these rites as installing or acknowledging the spirit's ritual position (Keightley 1978, pp. 165–175; Allan 2007, pp. 1–21).

### 3.2 Temples and the temple-name system

The Shang institutionalized ancestor deification through the *temple name* (庙号) system. Each deceased king received a “celestial stem” designation (甲, 乙, 丙…) that scheduled him into a rotating sacrificial calendar: ancestors were not merely remembered but *installed* in temples and served on fixed days. Keightley's reconstruction of the Shang five-ritual cycle (乡, 翌, 祭, �aci…) demonstrates a bureaucratic timetable by which the entire ancestral collectivity received graduated sacrifices appropriate to their divine rank (Keightley 1978, pp. 175–200; 2012, pp. xxi–xl).

The royal cemetery at Xibeigang, with its shaft tombs and surface ritual structures, provides archaeological correlates: the dead king was physically and ritually “seated” in a locale where ongoing cult could be performed (Bagley 1999, pp. 175–210; Tang 2001, pp. 165–173). Li Feng has argued that the ancestral temple was the central institution of Shang political authority—the seat of the god was the seat of legitimacy (Li 2006, pp. 28–42).

### 3.3 Ancestor seats and the high god Di (帝)

The Shang high god Di (帝) presided over an emergent divine bureaucracy. Ancestors served as intermediaries who could “di-announce” or intercede with Di. The graph Di itself (like 位 and the ritual “seat” graph) is built on an architectural/positional element, suggesting that divinity in Shang thought was conceptualized as enthronement. Allan reads Di's court as modeled on the royal court with Di “seated” above and ancestors approaching him as courtiers (Allan 1991, pp. 59–82; 2007, pp. 10–21).

---

## 4. Divination and the Confirmation of Ancestral Divinity

### 4.1 Pyroscapulimancy as epistemic technology

The oracle bone divination (卜 bǔ) was the third mechanism: through cracking ox scapulae and turtle plastrons, the Shang king queried ancestors and other powers and read their answers. Divination thus functioned as continuous verification of ancestral agency: the ancestors were gods precisely because they responded—sending dreams, illness, harvest failure, or military success—and the king confirmed the linkage through repeated charges (“It is Ancestor Jia who is harming [the king]?”).

Keightley has analyzed the “charge and verification” structure of inscriptions, showing that the appended verification notes (“after 31 days the king fell ill; the verification was auspicious”) closed the loop of divine communication (Keightley 1978, pp. 32–46). The very act of inscribing the bone and archiving it in pits constituted a record that an ancestor had spoken (Keightley 1978, pp. 47–62).

### 4.2 Diagnosing ancestral anger

A large class of inscriptions is diagnostic: the king was ill, the harvest was poor, the campaign stalled—and divination identified which ancestor caused it, followed by sacrifice to propitiate. This iterative cycle—misfortune, divination, identification, sacrifice, confirmation—operationalized divinity. The dead became gods by being causally effective and by being ritually legible (Keightley 2000, pp. 82–102; Campbell 2018, pp. 344–366).

### 4.3 Divination as royal monopoly

Chang's argument that the Shang king monopolized the means of communication with the ancestors (Chang 1983, pp. 21–45) is central: deification was controlled from the top. Only the king's lineage's ancestors became high gods with temple names and calendrical cults; deification was thus political theology. Robin Yates, Adam Smith, and others have shown how the divination script itself, standardized under Wu Ding and his successors, created a permanent divine archive (Smith 2011, pp. 1–14; Itō 1962, vol. 1, pp. 193–206).

---

## 5. Synthesis: The Bureaucracy of the Dead

The three mechanisms—figure, seat, and divination—were mutually reinforcing:

1. **Materialization** gave ancestors a locus in vessels, figures, tablets, and impersonators;
2. **Seating** gave them rank, place, and calendrical service within the temple system;
3. **Divination** gave them voice, verified their power, and archived their cult.

This system had profound political consequences. The king was defined as the one who could successfully serve the gods; the ancestors were defined as gods by being served. The Zhou conquest inherited and reworked this model, replacing Di's unpredictable will with Tian's moral order and recasting the ancestor-king relationship in the ideology of “virtue” (Shaughnessy 1999, pp. 1–32; Puett 2002, pp. 51–81). Michael Puett has argued that Shang and early Zhou practices treated ancestors as genuinely dangerous divine beings requiring ritual management, not sentimental commemoration (Puett 2002, pp. 29–81)—and it was precisely the manufactured, verified character of Shang ancestor-gods that made ritual an instrument of state.

---

## 6. Conclusion

Ancestor deification in the Shang was an administered process. The court made gods by making figures, seating them in temples with names and calendars, and confirming through divination that they heard, answered, and harmed. In this sense the Shang did not simply *believe* in divine ancestors; they *manufactured* them, and the oracle bone archive is the production log of that manufacture.

In "Defying the Law of Gravity: The Political Economy of International Migration" (*International Organization*, 2014), David Fitzgerald, David Leblang, and Sonia Whalley argue that migration cannot be adequately explained by "gravity" models alone—that is, models that predict migration flows based on factors like geographic distance, population size, and income differentials between countries.

Their central claim is that **migration is fundamentally network-driven**. Prospective migrants rely heavily on existing social networks—family members, friends, and co-ethnics already living abroad—to shape their decisions about where to go. These networks matter in several ways:

1. **Information provision**: Networks provide information about job prospects, living conditions, and legal channels at destination, reducing uncertainty.
2. **Cost reduction**: Established diasporas lower the material costs of migration by offering housing, jobs, financial support, and help navigating travel and legal barriers.
3. **Path dependence**: Because of these networks, migration flows become self-reinforcing over time—once a critical mass of migrants from a given origin establishes itself in a destination, future migrants disproportionately choose that same destination, even when other destinations might look equally or more attractive on paper.

Empirically, they show that adding measures of existing migrant stocks and network connections to standard gravity models substantially improves the ability to predict bilateral migration flows. In other words, migrants often "defy gravity" by traveling to culturally/network-connected destinations even when those places are far away or lack obvious economic advantages.

The broader implication is that migration patterns are largely a function of accumulated history and social relationships rather than simply responding to current economic incentives or geographic proximity—and that policies trying to manage migration flows will struggle if they ignore these network dynamics.

# 3D Design & Tech Stack Recommendation

## Part 1: The 3D Design Approach

There are two fundamentally different routes for your "AI metahumans with headphones" concept, and choosing between them changes everything downstream.

### Option A: Pre-rendered cinematic (what your brief describes)

This is the route your brief actually outlines — working with a 3D artist to perfect lighting/colour, render out the visual, and map camera movement to scroll.

**Recommended tools:**

- **Unreal Engine 5 + MetaHuman Creator** — This is the strongest fit for your brief. MetaHuman gives you photoreal AI-subject characters quickly, and UE5's Lumen lighting, Sequencer for camera paths, and real-time preview with GL make art-direction iteration fast. Render the scene as a **video sequence (e.g., 8–10 seconds, 60fps)** and scrub it via scroll.
- **Blender + BlenderKit / Human Generator** — A cheaper/free alternative. Blender's Cycles renderer can achieve comparable quality, and Geometry Nodes help with the "sci-fi garment" look. Slower iteration loop than UE5.
- **Character Creator (Reallusion) + iClone** — Middle ground; good for stylised-futuristic characters and exports cleanly to Unreal or Blender.

**Why pre-rendered wins here:**
- Photoreal metahumans in-browser (real-time WebGL) is still very hard to achieve convincingly without enormous optimisation effort.
- Lighting, colour grading, and post-processing (bloom, grain, chromatic aberration) will look dramatically better baked into a render.
- The "subtle animations" — headphones pumping, idle sway, butterflies — are trivial in a DCC tool, expensive in real-time WebGL.

### How the scroll-scrubbing works technically

- Render the camera path as an **image sequence or MP4**, then use a lightweight library like **ScrollMagic** or **GSAP ScrollTrigger** with a canvas to scrub frame-by-frame based on scroll position.
- Alternatively use Apple AirPods Pro-style **video scrubbing** (seek a muted video's currentTime on scroll) — simplest and most performant.
- Two renders as you specified: a tall/portrait-oriented render for desktop scroll behaviour, and your 16:9 variant for mobile. Detect device at the edge (server-side via user-agent, or serve `<picture>`/source switching) and load the appropriate sequence.

### Option B: Real-time 3D (Three.js / React Three Fiber)

Only worth considering if you want **interactive 360° camera control, parallax, or draggable inspection** of the subjects. Real-time gives:
- True scroll-mapped camera in 3D space (not just scrubbing footage)
- Device-orientation on mobile

But the tradeoffs are severe for photoreal humans:
- Realistic metahumans need heavy geometry, 4K+ textures, subsurface scattering shaders, HDRIs — expect 50–150MB+ payloads unless you invest heavily in optimisation (Draco compression, KTX2 textures, LODs).
- Stylised/treatment-heavy characters (strong post-processing, grain, fog, silhouette lighting) can work real-time and would reduce the "uncanny" risk of near-photoreal humans rendered poorly in a browser.

**My recommendation: go with Option A (pre-rendered scrub).** It matches the brief, guarantees art quality, performs well on low-end devices, and dramatically simplifies the build. Many award-winning sites (e.g., AirPods Pro page) use exactly this technique.

---

## Part 2: Is Next.js (React) the right framework?

**Yes — it's a strong, correct choice**, with these caveats and justifications:

**Why Next.js fits:**
1. **Server-side rendering** — critical for SEO on the tagline copy points and the two static content pages. A pure client-side WebGL site often ships an empty DOM; Next.js solves this.
2. **Route structure** — 3 distinct pages (main scroll experience + 2 static pages) maps cleanly to the App Router.
3. **Performance features** — image optimisation, code-splitting, and streaming all help with heavy video assets (Next's `next/image` and video lazy-loading).
4. **If you later go real-time 3D**, **React Three Fiber + drei** integrates natively with Next.js, so you keep optionality.

**Caveats / recommendations:**
- Use the **App Router with static export (SSG)** if the site is purely marketing — no need for a Node server, deploy to Vercel/Netlify as static files for maximum speed.
- Handle the scroll experience **client-side only** (`'use client'` components, GSAP ScrollTrigger) while keeping tagline text server-rendered for SEO.
- **Preload the video/sequence carefully** — use `preload="auto"`, host on a CDN, and consider serving a low-res placeholder first, then swapping to the full render once buffered.
- Consider **MP4 with `requestVideoFrameCallback`** scrubbing rather than PNG sequences — PNG sequences at 60fps × hundreds of frames can total 100MB+; modern MP4/H.264 (or HEVC/AV1 with fallback) is far lighter.
- Beware **iOS Safari quirks** with video scrubbing (limit seeks, use muted+playsinline) — this is exactly why your separate 16:9 mobile render is a good idea.

# Caught

The sun was setting over this world's forest, painting everything in shades of amber and gold, and I was walking back to camp with a pocketful of interesting rocks.

I know how that sounds. A cyborg from a technologically advanced parallel dimension, part machine, chrome plating visible along my left forearm and up the side of my neck, and I was collecting rocks. But in my defense, these rocks were *interesting*. One of them faintly glowed when I held it up to the light, and Henry was going to lose his mind over it. He'd been cataloguing local minerals since we arrived three days ago, and so far his journal entries had all been variations on "I don't understand this place and it's wonderful."

That was the general consensus among the five of us, honestly. Ethan, our team leader, had been initially skeptical about the whole "magic dimension" thing until he watched a woman in the market town literally levitate a cart out of a ditch. Olivia had filled two sketchbooks. Lucas kept trying to get locals to explain the rules of their magic and kept getting answers like "it works because it does, isn't that lovely?" which was slowly driving him insane.

Me? I kept to myself mostly. Always had. Back home, people saw the machinery integrated into my body and got either nervous or overly fascinated, and I'd learned early that quiet observation was easier than conversation. My team was the exception—they'd long since stopped seeing the metal and just saw me—but strangers? I liked to keep a low profile. Which, admittedly, was harder to do when your left arm was partially chrome in a world that hadn't invented the steam engine yet. I'd taken to wearing my jacket with the sleeves pulled down and my hood up whenever I went into town.

Anyway. Rocks. Sunset. Forest path. I was maybe a mile out from camp when everything went sideways.

I was thinking about dinner—Olivia had promised something with those purple tubers she'd traded for—when my foot snagged on something that definitely wasn't a root.

I remember thinking, very calmly, *tripwire*, and then the world exploded into motion. Ropes whipped up from the leaf litter on either side of the path—one snaring my ankles, two more winding around my arms—and a counterweight somewhere above me dropped with a groan of rope through pulley. The whole contraption yanked me off my feet and slammed me flat on my back in the dirt, arms pinned to my sides, legs bound together, staring up at the canopy.

"Ow," I said, to no one.

I lay there for a moment, running diagnostics. Nothing damaged. My backplate had taken the brunt of the impact. The ropes were impressively engineered, actually—woven, waxed, anchored at multiple points. Whomever had built this knew what they were doing.

I wriggled experimentally. Nope. Properly stuck.

In the interests of honesty, I'll admit my first thought was not *danger* or *ambush* or even *what's going on*. My first thought was, *huh, this happens sometimes.* In our line of work—dimensional survey and exploration—you eventually get jumped by just about everything. Lucas got netted by tree people in the second world we visited. Olivia was once carried off by something with too many wings and had to be traded back for a box of chocolate bars. Ethan got mugged in the fourth world by a gang of children who couldn't have been older than ten, and honestly never lived it down. Getting trapped in a forest was practically a rite of passage.

So I sighed, relaxed into the dirt, and waited for whatever came next. Probably bandits. Possibly wildlife. Maybe a curious local. I'd figure it out when it showed up.

What showed up was a young woman stepping out from behind a tree about twenty feet down the path, and my processors did that little stutter they do when something doesn't compute.

She had light blue hair. Not dyed-looking blue—a soft, natural blue that fell past her shoulders, catching the sunset light like water. Her eyes matched, bright and blue and absolutely *delighted* at the moment. She was dressed well—finely, actually, embroidered bodice, clean boots, a small silver circlet that she'd hidden under a hood that was now pushed back. She was also, I noticed, holding a length of rope and grinning at me like I was a wrapped present.

"You fell for it!" she said, and she sounded genuinely thrilled. "You walked right into the middle of the snare. Most of them step on the edge and only get one leg, but you got everything. Both arms! I've never caught anyone so completely on the first day."

"Congratulations," I said. "That's... a thing to be proud of, I guess. Nice trap. Very well engineered."

That made her pause. She tilted her head, blue hair spilling over one shoulder. "You're not angry?"

"I mean, I wasn't planning on lying in the dirt this evening, but I've had worse Tuesdays." I tested the ropes again, more out of habit than hope. "Are you with the bandits, or is this a shakedown, or...?"

"Bandits?" Her nose wrinkled. "Absolutely not. I am Princess Seraphina, third child of King Aldric of Verdholm." She said this with the casual confidence of someone announcing that water is wet, then she walked over and crouched down beside me, studying me like a specimen. "And you are the strangest thing I've ever caught."

"Caught," I repeated. "You keep using that word. Also, princess? You set traps yourself? Don't you have people for that?"

"My father has trappers," she said, "but they're terrible at this particular kind, and I wanted to do it myself." She'd produced a small knife and was cutting the rope at my ankles, though the ones binding my arms stayed firmly in place. "There. You can sit up."

I managed to get myself upright with some effort, which mostly involved doing an awkward abdominal curl since my arms were still lashed to my sides. I ended up sitting in the middle of the path, legs stretched out in front of me, looking up at a blue-haired princess who was circling me with her hands clasped behind her back.

"So," she said slowly, circling. "Questions."

"Same," I said. "Starting with the big one."

"All in time." She stopped in front of me and leaned down, peering at my face. "First—what are you wearing? I've never seen cloth like that. It's stitched so strangely, all these little perfect lines."

I looked down at myself. Right. My jeans, oil-stained from working on my own knee servos two days ago, and my jacket hood, which had come down in the fall. "It's just... pants? Denim. And a jacket."

"De-nim." She pronounced it carefully, like tasting a foreign word. "And these stains—smith's grease? Are you a smith?"

"Sort of, kind of. I do metalwork." Not a lie, technically. I do a *lot* of metalwork on myself.

"And your manner of speaking." She crouched again, elbows on her knees, chin in her hands. "You talk like nobody from around here. You're calm as a pond, you just got trapped in a forest by a princess, and you're chatting with me like we've met at a garden party. Who *are* you?"

"Leam," I said. "I'm from... very far away. My friends and I are traveling through, studying the land. That's honest, I promise."

"Leam." She tried the name out. "Leam. That's a good name. Strong." Then her eyes drifted, and I realized my sleeve had ridden up in the fall, exposing the chrome plating of my forearm glinting in the dying light.

Her eyes went wide. "What is *that?*"

I looked at my arm. Then at her. "It's... a prosthesis? An artificial limb. I was in an accident, and this is how they fixed me."

She reached out and then hesitated, looking up at me for permission. I nodded, and she touched the back of my forearm with one fingertip, then more boldly, running her fingers over the smooth metal. "It's warm," she said, startled.

"There's synthetic musculature in there. Fake muscle, basically. Runs warm."

"Fake muscle. In fake metal." She said it flatly, the way people say things when they're deciding whether to believe you. "Where you come from, do they build people?"

"Sometimes, yeah. Where I come from, we build a lot of things." I decided to ease her into it. "We don't have magic where I'm from, but we have machines that can fly between cities in hours, lights that glow without flame, boxes that let you talk to someone on the other side of the world..."

She snorted, which surprised me. "Talking boxes. You're teasing me."

"I'm really not."

"A machine that flies? With no magic at all? Birds fly because of wind-magic, everyone knows that."

"It's the shape of the wing, mostly. Air pressure. It's—" I stopped. "It's a long explanation."

She was smiling now, and I was starting to realize something about this girl: she was mischievous. It was all over her face, in the crinkle of her eyes, in the way she'd trapped me and then immediately got distracted by my clothes. She was the kind of person who did things because they were interesting, and right now, I was the most interesting thing in the forest.

"Okay," I said, "my turn. The trap. What's the trap *for?* Because if this is a kidnapping, I have four friends back at camp who are going to have questions, and if it's a robbery, I should warn you my rocks are only medium-good."

She laughed, a bright, startled sound. "Rocks?"

"I found one that glows."

"Show me later." She waved this off and then—and this is the part where the evening took a turn—she sat down *right next to me*, close enough that our shoulders were almost touching, and said, matter-of-fact as anything:

"The trap is for my husband."

I blinked. "I'm sorry?"

"Marriage," she said pleasantly. "Here, that's how it's done. A woman who wants to be married builds a snare and catches a man with it. Whatever she catches, she keeps. It's tradition. My grandmother caught my grandfather in a net off the eastern road. My mother caught my father during a hunt—he says he never even saw the pit coming, which everyone agrees was very romantic."

I stared at her. She stared back, serene.

"So you..." I looked down at the ropes binding my arms. The ropes binding my arms. The trap. The marriage trap. "So this trap—"

"Is our wedding," she finished cheerfully. "Yes. Well. The first part. There are ceremonies after, but those are just decoration. The snare is the real marriage. You fall, I catch, you're mine." She tilted her head. "Congratulations, by the way. You were very elegant about it. Most men shout."

Somewhere in the back of my mind, I heard Lucas's voice: *every world has different customs, and it's our job to respect them.* And then right behind it, the rest of my mind, which was doing the equivalent of sirens and flashing lights.

"Okay," I said, slowly. "Okay. I want to be really clear that I'm not angry, I'm just... processing. In your world, the way you get married is by trapping a stranger in the woods."

"By trapping your *chosen* stranger in the woods," she corrected. "You don't catch just anyone. You build the snare in the place where the man you want walks. I've been watching the paths east of the river for three days, and then this afternoon, along you come—dressed like a mad tinker, talking to yourself about dinner, strolling right down the *center* of the path like you've never heard of a rope in your life." She sighed happily. "It was meant to be."

"I was talking about tubers," I said weakly. "I wasn't—that's not—"

"And then," she went on, warming to it, "you fell into it *perfectly*, and then instead of shouting you said *nice trap, very well engineered*—" she mimicked my tone with startling accuracy— "and I thought, well, that's that decided, then."

"Decided? What's decided? Nothing's decided!"

She shifted closer. I felt her shoulder press against mine, warm through my jacket. "I decided to keep you," she said, as though this were a completely reasonable thing to announce. "You're funny, and strange, and you're not scared of me, and you have a *warm metal arm* which I still don't fully believe in, and you're rather handsome under all that hood, which—" she reached up and pulled my hood fully down, fingers ruffling through my hair, "—yes. Definitely keeping you."

Now, I want it on the record that I am not easily flustered. I have been shot at in four different dimensions. I once had a very reasonable conversation with a creature made mostly of eyes. I keep to myself, I keep my cool, it's kind of my whole thing.

I felt my face heat up so fast I was worried my thermal sensors would flag it.

"That's—" My voice did something embarrassing in the middle of the word. I cleared my throat. "That's not how it works. Where I'm from. Marriage, I mean. Where I'm from, you—there's courtship, and asking, and both people have to agree, there's a whole *mutual* thing, it's very involved—"

"Both people agree?" She looked intrigued rather than deterred. Her fingers were still in my hair, and I was becoming extremely aware of that. She was combing through it slowly, like she was learning the texture of it. "But how do you know who to ask?"

"You just... know? You spend time with someone, and you like them, and eventually one of you asks."

"That sounds *terrifying*," Seraphina said with full sincerity. "All that knowing and asking and agreeing. What if you're wrong? What if you ask and they say no? With the snare, there's no wondering. The rope decides."

"The rope decided," I repeated. "The rope. An inanimate object made the most important decision of your life."

"The rope, the woman who built it, the man who walked into it," she said, ticking them off. "It's a partnership between craft and fate." She leaned her head against my shoulder, settling in like we'd been married for years instead of eleven minutes. "Honestly, most girls catch someone they've liked from town for ages. The snare's just the formal part. I'm doing it properly backward, catching a complete stranger, but my sister says I overthink everything, so."

"You caught a complete *stranger* and you're already—look, could you not do the hair thing, it's very—" I was babbling. I never babble. "It's distracting."

"Mm, I noticed," she said, delighted, and did it more.

"Why do you marry like this?" I asked, which was maybe the first coherent question I'd managed in several minutes. "Here, I mean. Why traps? Who looked at a snare and thought, romance?"

She laughed against my shoulder. "It's old. Older than the kingdom. The way Grandmother tells it, in the old days, men were hunters and spent all their time in the woods, and if a girl wanted one, she had to beat him at his own game. The snare proved she was clever enough and strong enough to keep him safe, keep him fed, keep his household. It's not about capturing him, really, it's about proving you can." She looked up at me, and there was something underneath the mischief now—something steady and sure. "A man worth having is a man worth building a good trap for."

"And you built... that." I nodded down the path at the wreckage of the snare. "The ropes, the counterweight, the multiple anchor points."

"I watched the trappers for two seasons," she said, with quiet pride. "I built eleven versions before this one."

"You built *eleven*—"

"Practice snares. In the castle garden. My brother fell into four of them, which he was *not* happy about."

Despite everything—despite the ropes and the absurdity and the fact that I was technically at this moment a married man by the legal standards of a world I'd been in for three days—I laughed. Actually laughed. She beamed like I'd handed her a present.

"There," she said. "I knew I'd keep you when you made that face. You laugh like you weren't expecting to."

"I wasn't," I admitted. "Expecting any of this. I was expecting tubers."

"The evening's not over." She reached over and, with that same small knife, cut the ropes binding my arms in three efficient motions. I rubbed my wrists as the circulation re-established itself, half expecting her to have some second phase of the trap. She didn't. She just sat there, hands folded in her lap, watching me with those blue, blue eyes.

"You're free to go," she said. "You could walk away right now, and it'd be as if nothing happened. Nobody would even call it a real marriage if the man ran off. That happens sometimes, and it's a terrible embarrassment for the girl, so." She lifted her chin. There was the determination under everything—quiet and iron. "So I'm telling you I'm letting you loose, and you can choose. But I'd like it very much if you didn't run."

I looked down the path. Camp was a mile that way. Olivia was probably cooking. Lucas would want my opinion on the magic-is-energy hypothesis. It was, objectively, where I belonged.

I looked at the princess with blue hair sitting patiently in the leaf litter, hands folded, watching me with hope she was trying very hard not to show.

"Your world is unbelievable," I said.

"You haven't seen a tenth of it."

"My team is going to have so many questions."

"Then we should go answer them." She popped to her feet and offered me a hand up. I took it—her grip was strong, calloused in the way you don't expect from a princess—and found myself standing face to face with her.

# Globalization, GVCs, and Pandemic-Era Supply Shortages: A Balanced Assessment

## Was Globalization/GVCs the "Cause" of Shortages?

**The case against blaming GVCs alone:**

The evidence suggests globalization was more of an **amplifier** than the root cause of shortages:

- **Demand shocks mattered more than supply chain fragility.** The shortage of PPE, ventilators, and medicines was driven largely by an unprecedented 100–1,000-fold surge in demand, which no production system—domestic or foreign—could have absorbed instantly.
- **Domestic supply failed too.** Countries with substantial domestic pharmaceutical production (the US, India, Germany) still faced shortages because they imported *inputs* (active pharmaceutical ingredients, APIs) and because domestic capacity was sized for normal demand, not crises.
- **Trade restrictions were the real culprit in many cases.** Export bans (e.g., India's restrictions on APIs and medicines, various PPE export controls) fragmented supply more than interdependence itself did. Globalization created channels; **policy responses choked them**.
- **Concentration, not globalization per se.** The problem was often extreme geographic concentration (e.g., China producing a large share of APIs and masks) driven by efficiency-seeking consolidation—governments and firms chose low-cost, just-in-time resilience over redundancy.

**The case for some blame:**

- Just-in-time inventory and lean production left no buffer stocks.
- Offshoring hollowed out domestic surge capacity and the industrial ecosystem (skilled workers, auxiliary suppliers) needed to scale up quickly.
- Long, opaque chains made it hard to know where vulnerabilities lay.

## Is Reshoring the Best Answer?

**Shortcomings of reshoring as a strategy:**

1. **It doesn't solve the surge-capacity problem.** Even fully domestic production sized for normal demand fails during a pandemic-scale demand shock unless countries hold strategic reserves or maintain idle capacity—expensive under any ownership arrangement.
2. **Higher costs and reduced efficiency.** Reshoring everything means paying more for goods year-round to insure against rare events; that trade-off is rarely cost-effective for most products.
3. **No country can be fully self-sufficient.** Medical goods require dozens of inputs (APIs, precursors, specialty chemicals, components). Full supply-chain sovereignty is practically impossible at reasonable cost.
4. **Reshoring one link doesn't de-risk the chain.** You may relocate final assembly but still depend on imported intermediates.

**Better approaches:**

- **Diversification over repatriation**: "China+1" strategies, multiple sourcing countries, and friend-shoring reduce single-point-of-failure risk.
- **Strategic stockpiles and surge capacity**: maintaining reserves of critical items and agreements with manufacturers for rapid scale-up (the ROI on stockpiles proved far better than the cost of shortages).
- **International cooperation and trade disciplines**: agreements to keep critical medical supply chains open during crises (avoiding export-ban beggar-thy-neighbor policies), as pursued in WTO/G20 discussions.
- **Transparency and mapping**: knowing where chokepoints exist (e.g., via supply-chain mapping and "stress tests").
- **Targeted, not blanket, reshoring**: reserve reshoring for a narrow list of truly critical, low-volume items where domestic capacity is feasible (e.g., certain APIs or vaccines).

## Conclusion

Globalization and GVCs were **not the primary culprit**—the pandemic exposed a governance failure (no preparedness, no stockpiles, no rules against export restrictions) and a demand shock that no system could easily meet. Reshoring is **not** the best or sufficient answer: it is costly, often infeasible, and doesn't address surge demand or input dependencies. The more promising strategy is **resilience through diversification, redundancy (stockpiles/surge capacity), transparency, and international coordination**, with selective, targeted localization only for the most critical goods where the security benefits clearly outweigh the costs.

# Tehran Bookstore Reopens on Valiasr Street After Evacuation of Saadat Abad Location

TEHRAN — Shafaq Book House, forced to cease operations in Tehran's Saadat Abad district, will resume business at a new location on Valiasr Street at its intersection with Zarasht Street, its manager said.

Mohammad Taqi Haqbein told the Iran Book News Agency (IBNA) that the bookstore had been compelled to vacate its former premises four days ago. He said the property's owner had notified the business in April that it would have to leave, prompting a search for suitable quarters that culminated in the acquisition of the Valiasr Street site.

Haqbein noted an irony in the transition: the new premises housed a restaurant chain for 15 years before its conversion into a bookstore — a reversal, he observed, of the more familiar narrative in which bookshops are supplanted by restaurants and cafés.

The 370-square-meter space, Haqbein said, constitutes ample accommodation for the enterprise. Renovation and equipping are underway, and he expressed hope that the bookstore could host its inaugural gathering of bibliophiles by the end of July.

Haqbein urged the government to attend to the exigencies of a new generation of booksellers, calling for concessional facilities that would enable their continued operation and safeguard their viability. He advocated enforcement of existing legislation that extends support to cultural institutions for operational expenditures such as water, electricity and gas.

"The previous generation of booksellers owns their stores and consequently faces fewer challenges than their successors, who must contend with rental obligations," he said. "For that reason, I believe the new generation merits commensurate support."

Haqbein also disclosed that through the efforts of private-sector activists, approximately 5,000 square meters of additional retail space will be added this year to bookstore storefronts across the country.

According to IBNA, Shafaq Book House operated in the Saadat Abad district for seven years before its evacuation and closure four days ago at the behest of the building's owner.

# MDX Food International Unveils... the Orange?! A Launch Event for the Ages

DUBAI, UAE — April 13th, 2023. Mark it. Remember it. Because on that strangely momentous morning, in the unlikely grandeur of the Knowledge Village Courtyard (9:00–10:15 am, sharp), MDX Food International — self-proclaimed titan of fresh food distribution — did the unthinkable: they launched the orange.

Yes. The orange.

You know the one. Round. Citrus-y. Sitting innocently in your grandmother's fruit bowl since roughly the dawn of civilization. But hold your skepticism — because MDX FI, ever the trailblazer in "discovering" and globalizing fresh foods (their words, not ours), declared this a milestone. A *significant* one.

The festivities opened with a skit — a theatrical retelling of *how the orange was created*, which raises some genuinely fascinating metaphysical questions the company has yet to answer. An announcer followed, expressing gratitude to the sizable crowd who apparently had a free hour and change on a Thursday morning.

Then came the CEO. His speech touched on freshness, nutrition, quality, global reach — the standard greatest hits — before piveting, somewhat remarkably, to child labor allegations. He assured attendees the matter was taken "seriously" and that suppliers now adhere to "strict ethical standards." Bold move, addressing that at a fruit launch. Almost admirable, honestly. Then: scissors, ribbon, snip — the orange was officially *introduced to the world*, as if it had been hiding in a cave for millennia, waiting for this precise moment.

A product video followed, cataloguing the orange's many varieties and their "unique characteristics." (Some are sweeter. Some are more sour. Groundbreaking stuff.)

Behind the scenes, chaos: a TikTok influencer, slated as brand ambassador, ghosted the event at the eleventh hour. Undaunted, the company's sponsored athlete stepped in, heroically covering *both* roles — presumably doubling the Instagram stories and the athletic endorsement in one fell swoop.

From there, the event careened gloriously onward: a "mad scientist" (again, their words) presented the product line; a product tester demonstrated zest, juicing, culinary applications, and the stunning revelation that — brace yourself — *all parts* of the orange can be used. A sports person (distinct, apparently, from the athlete ambassador) connected oranges to athletic performance, citing health benefits with the conviction of someone who'd been handed talking points an hour earlier.

The finale? Musical hot potato. With a prize. The crowd, reportedly, loved it.
