# Alternate Ending: "Go Goo Go" and Beyond

## The Confession

After Mac apologizes for yelling at her, Goo hugs him tightly—and something shifts. Mac's face goes crimson as he realizes his heart is racing. He pulls away quickly, stammering something about checking on Bloo, and practically sprints off.

*What was that?* he thinks. *She's just Goo. Loud, chaotic, imaginary-friend-creating Goo. I can't... no. Absolutely not.*

But the damage is done. Mac spends the next week avoiding her, making excuses, and failing miserably at acting normal. What he doesn't notice is the sly, knowing little smile Goo wears every time he trips over his own words—she caught the look on his face the moment they pulled apart.

---

## "The Big Picture"

The annual house photo is chaos as usual—imaginary friends arguing over positions, Mr. Herriman demanding order, Bloo insisting on center stage. Mac is distracted, hyper-aware of Goo's presence as she "helps" by creating a lighting expert, a costume designer, and a "vibe coordinator."

When they discover the strange old photo of Foster's, Mac and Bloo investigate. Goo joins them, and Mac can't focus on the mystery because she keeps grabbing his arm whenever she spots a clue.

"Look, Mac! This shadow proves someone was standing behind the founder!"

Mac's face burns. "Y-yeah. Great detecting. Can you maybe... personal space?"

Goo tilts her head innocently. "But we're friends! Friends don't need personal space!"

*Friends. Right. Just friends,* Mac thinks miserably.

Bloo smirks. "What's wrong with you? You're acting weirder than usual."

"Nothing! Shut up!"

---

## "Neighbor Pains"

Adopt-A-Thought Saturday arrives, and Goo's organizational skills are genuinely helpful—she's created imaginary friends whose entire purpose is managing logistics. Mac tries to keep his distance, but every time he turns around, she's there, cheerfully directing traffic or helping frightened imaginary friends feel brave.

"Mac! Look, I made a filing system!"

"That's... really good, Goo," he admits, genuinely impressed.

Her face lights up. "You think so?!"

Before he can stop himself, he smiles. "Yeah. You're actually pretty amazing at this."

Goo freezes, then beams so brightly his heart stutters. He immediately retreats, muttering about helping Wilt.

Bloo watches from nearby. "You've got it bad, man."

"I don't know what you're talking about."

---

## "Infernal Slumber"

The surprise slumber party is already stressful—keeping a pile of imaginary friends quiet in a tiny apartment on a school night. But Mac's real problem is that Goo is *right there*, in oversized mismatched pajamas, whispering loudly about creating a "silent but fun" imaginary friend for the occasion.

"No, Goo, don't create anything! My mom will hear!"

"Don't worry! My new friend is invisible AND inaudible!"

"That's not how—" Mac gives up, collapsing next to her. She pats his head sympathetically.

"You work too hard, Mac. You should relax more."

Her hand lingers in his hair, and his brain short-circuits. He jumps up, hits his head on the coffee table, and hisses in pain.

"Ow! I'm fine! Everything's fine!"

When the gang has to cram into the closet to hide from his mom, Goo ends up squished against Mac's chest. He bites his own hand to keep from making a sound, face glowing neon red in the dark.

"Cozy, huh?" Goo whispers right into his ear.

Mac nods furiously, entirely incapable of speech, praying his hammering heartbeat isn't echoing through the whole apartment.

---

Mac spends the whole episode trying to prevent a surprise party. But every time Goo approaches him with a smile, his defenses scramble. When she corners him in a hallway to give him something, he panics.

## "The Big Cheese"

With the new alarm system and Cheese causing chaos, everyone gets locked out—and only Cheese knows the code. Goo steps in, patiently working with Cheese and creating an imaginary friend who speaks "Cheese" to translate his babble.

Mac watches her with an undeniably dreamy expression, transfixed by her kindness and patience. Bloo has to snap his fingers in front of his face three times.

"Mac, stop staring at Goo like she's a giant bowl of sugar and help me shake the door!"

"I WASN'T STARING!" Mac shouts, voice cracking.

Goo cracks the code, turns around, and catches Mac frantically pretending to inspect a crack in the wall. She grins knowingly. Later, when she successfully decodes the alarm, Mac grabs her in a celebratory hug without thinking—then lets go, face red.

"I—that was—good job!"

Goo blinks, then grins. "You hugged me!"

"It was a celebratory hug! For the team! For everyone!"

---

## "Make Believe It or Not"

When Goo's imaginary game villains come to life and imprison Mac and Bloo, Mac is sick with worry—not for himself, but for her. When Goo finally bursts in with heroic imaginary creatures to defeat the villains, Mac doesn't even care about the chaos. He throws his arms around her.

"Goo! You're okay!"

Realizing what he's doing, he jumps back three paces. "I mean—statistically, your survival was probable, but—tactically speaking, good rescue!"

Goo crosses her arms, smiling fondly. "Sure, Mac. Purely tactical."

---

## "Schlock Star"

When Bloo forms his rival band, Goo volunteers as MC—energetic, enthusiastic, and genuinely supportive of everyone. Mac watches from the crowd, unable to take his eyes off her.

"You're staring," Frankie whispers, appearing beside him.

"I'm not staring. I'm... observing. As a friend."

"Uh-huh. Sure."

Right before the show, Mac nervously approaches Goo backstage. "Hey, Goo... you're doing a really good job. You're really brave. I'd be terrified in front of all those people."

Goo smiles warmly, stepping close to straighten his collar. "Thanks, Mac. It's easy when you know your favorite person is in the audience."

She bounds onstage, leaving Mac frozen backstage, clutching his chest over the phrase *favorite person*.

---

## "Goodbye to Bloo"

When the misunderstanding spreads that Mac is moving away forever, the gang throws an elaborate farewell. Goo sings a nonsensical song full of rhyming vegetables and random noises—seemingly oblivious to the solemn tragedy Bloo is orchestrating.

Then the truth comes out. "I'M NOT MOVING AWAY! My mom just got a promotion! She needs a home office, so we're moving to a bigger apartment in the exact same building! Two floors up! That's it!"

As the friends collapse in relief and annoyance, Mac slips away to the balcony to catch his breath. The door clicks open. Goo walks out, the evening breeze blowing her wild hair.

"I knew, you know," she says quietly.

Mac blinks. "You... knew we were just moving upstairs?"

"Well, yeah—your mom mentioned it to my mom last week," Goo giggles. "Why do you think I sang that ridiculous song? I was just playing along with Bloo's drama." Then her expression softens, turning uncharacteristically still. "And I know about the other thing, too."

Mac swallows hard. "What other thing?"

"Mac." She steps closer. "You've been turning redder than your shirt every time I stand next to you for *months*. You trip over your own feet when I smile, you panic every time I hug you, and you defend me before Bloo can even finish an insult."

The urge to deny it rises in his throat—*it's just Foster's dust, I'm just clumsy*—but looking into her bright, patient eyes, he sees there's no use. She isn't laughing at him. She's just... waiting.

He lets out a long, defeated exhale. A furious blush creeps up his neck, but this time he doesn't look at his shoes.

"...How long have you known?"

Goo beams. "Since the day it rained on the porch. The day you apologized and I hugged you. Your heart was beating like a little hummingbird, Mac."

"And you didn't say anything?!"

"Of course not!" Goo laughs, grabbing his hands. "I wanted to see how long it would take for the smartest boy in the world to finally be honest. Plus... it was ridiculously cute."

Mac groans, burying his burning face in his hands—though a wide, helpless smile breaks through his fingers. "You're unbelievable, Goo."

"I'm imaginative!" she corrects cheerfully. She gently pulls his hands away and pecks him quickly on the cheek.

Mac's brain flatlines for three seconds.

"Awwww!" Bloo's voice rings out. The whole gang is crowded in the balcony doorway—Bloo smug, Wilt sighing, Eduardo in happy tears, Frankie grinning.

"How long have you been standing there?!" Mac yelps.

"Long enough!" Bloo cackles. "You owe me twenty bucks, Wilt!"

"I really thought he'd last another week," Wilt admits.

Mr. Herriman clears his throat. "While I am... pleased you have resolved your emotional turmoil, Mr. Mac, perhaps this could have been done without the public spectacle?"

Goo just laughs, still holding Mac's hand. "Where's the fun in that?"

"Come on, boyfriend," she chirps, tugging him toward the doors, already talking a mile a minute about the cake Bloo is about to demolish. "If we don't hurry he's gonna swallow the plastic figurines whole and Herriman will have to do the Heimlich and it'll be a whole huge mess—"

Mac stumbles after her, his cheek tingling, his hand firmly in hers. He still can't quite keep up with her—but for the first time, he's more than happy to try.

**THE END**

# Report: The Internet of Things and a Proposed Smart Irrigation Solution

## 1. Overview of the Internet of Things (IoT)

### What is it?

The Internet of Things (IoT) is a network of everyday physical objects—from household appliances to industrial machinery—that are fitted with sensors, software and network connectivity so they can collect and exchange data over the internet. These "smart objects" can sense their environment, report what they find, and in many cases act on it automatically. The central idea is to close the gap between the physical and digital worlds, making remote monitoring, control and automation possible on a very large scale.

### How does it work?

Most IoT systems follow a four-stage cycle:

1. **Sensing layer:** Devices such as sensors, cameras and actuators gather data from their surroundings—temperature, motion, humidity, soil moisture, heart rate and so on.
2. **Network layer:** The data is sent to a processing point using a suitable protocol: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Zigbee, cellular (4G/5G, NB-IoT) or long-range low-power options such as LoRaWAN.
3. **Processing layer:** A cloud platform or local server stores and analyses the data, often with machine-learning models that turn raw readings into useful insight.
4. **Application layer:** Results are shown to the user through a mobile app or web dashboard, and the system can trigger automatic actions (for example, switching on a pump) or send alerts for manual decisions.

### Advantages

- **Efficiency and automation:** Routine tasks are handled automatically, improving productivity in manufacturing, energy, logistics and agriculture.
- **Data-driven decisions:** Real-time data supports better choices than guesswork or outdated records.
- **Improved quality of life:** Smart homes, wearable health monitors and connected vehicles add convenience and safety.
- **Resource optimisation:** Smart grids and agricultural sensors help save water and energy.
- **Cost reduction:** Predictive maintenance avoids expensive breakdowns, and smarter inventory management cuts waste.

### Disadvantages

- **Security vulnerabilities:** Every connected device is a potential entry point for attackers, and many low-power devices have weak built-in security.
- **Privacy concerns:** Constant data collection raises questions about who owns the data and how it is used.
- **Complexity and interoperability:** Different vendors and protocols do not always work together smoothly.
- **Data overload:** The volume of data produced can be difficult and costly to store and analyse.
- **High setup cost:** Sensors, infrastructure and specialist skills require significant initial investment, especially at industrial scale.

### The future of IoT

IoT is converging with other technologies. **AI and machine learning** will make sense of the data and enable genuinely intelligent automation. **Edge computing**—processing data near the source—will cut latency and bandwidth use for real-time applications. **5G and beyond** will support far denser and more reliable device networks. **Digital twins**, virtual replicas of physical systems, will allow simulation and testing without risk. Security is also maturing, with hardware-based trust and automated key management becoming standard.

## 2. Problem Statement

Agriculture uses roughly 70% of global freshwater withdrawals, yet much of it is wasted. Many small and mid-sized farms still irrigate on fixed timers or by visual judgement, without regard to actual soil moisture or upcoming rain. The result is either **over-irrigation**—water loss through runoff and deep drainage, root disease, nutrient leaching and unnecessary pumping costs—or **under-irrigation**, which stresses plants and reduces yield. Climate change, with increasingly unpredictable rainfall, makes fixed schedules even less reliable. What is needed is an affordable, self-powered, closed-loop system that measures conditions in the field itself and waters only when the crop actually needs it.

## 3. Existing Solutions

- **Timer-based irrigation controllers:** Cheap and simple, but completely blind to weather and soil conditions, so they waste water during rain and under-water during heat waves.
- **Commercial precision-agriculture and SCADA systems:** Highly capable, but built around expensive controllers, trench wiring and proprietary software. Costs of thousands of dollars per installation put them out of reach for smaller farms, and their rigid design makes expansion difficult.
- **DIY sensor kits (Arduino/Raspberry Pi):** Affordable, but demand real technical skill to build and maintain, usually lack a proper user interface, and are often not robust enough for long-term field use.
- **Weather apps and manual moisture meters:** Weather apps give regional forecasts, not field-level conditions, and handheld meters provide only spot readings with no automation.

Each option is either too expensive, too complex or too limited, leaving a clear gap for an integrated, low-cost system.

## 4. Proposed Solution: "AgriPulse"

**AgriPulse** is a solar-powered, IoT-based autonomous irrigation system for small and mid-sized farms. Self-powered sensor nodes placed around the field measure soil moisture and local climate and send readings over long-range LoRa radio to an on-site edge controller. That controller decides when to water, taking into account the soil's water balance and the local rain forecast, and opens or closes the irrigation valves automatically. The farmer follows everything—and can override it—through a simple mobile or web dashboard. Because the core decisions are made locally, the system keeps working during internet outages.

## 5. Key Components

1. **Sensor nodes:** Each node contains a capacitive soil-moisture probe (more corrosion-resistant than cheap resistive probes), a temperature/humidity/pressure sensor (e.g. BME280), a low-power microcontroller with a LoRa radio (e.g. ESP32 with an SX1262 transceiver), and a small solar panel with battery for continuous off-grid operation.
2. **Edge controller (gateway):** Located at the farmstead, it receives data from all nodes, fetches a local weather forecast over the internet, runs the irrigation decision algorithm, and drives the valves through relay outputs.
3. **Actuation hardware:** Low-power latching solenoid valves connected through opto-isolated relays, so valves stay in position without drawing current.
4. **Cloud service and dashboard:** Stores historical data in a time-series database, provides charts and alerts, and lets the farmer set thresholds and override schedules remotely.

## 7. Conclusion

IoT turns ordinary objects into connected, data-producing systems, and its combination with edge computing and AI makes it especially valuable where decisions must be made quickly and locally. AgriPulse applies these ideas to one of agriculture's most pressing problems: wasteful irrigation. By measuring the soil directly, predicting the crop's water needs and automating the valves on site, it offers a practical, affordable and resilient alternative to fixed timers and expensive industrial systems, and a realistic step toward more sustainable water use on smaller farms.

# CHAPTER 1: INTRODUCTION

## 1.1 Background of the Study

Macroeconomic management in developing economies rests on two principal levers: fiscal policy, exercised by the government through taxation, public expenditure and debt, and monetary policy, conducted by the central bank through control of money supply, interest rates and reserve requirements. Neither lever operates in a vacuum. The effectiveness of one is contingent on the stance of the other, and the coherence—or conflict—between them is a decisive determinant of whether policy supports or undermines long-run economic development (Sargent & Wallace, 1981; Woodford, 2001). The Keynesian tradition stresses the role of countercyclical fiscal action in smoothing volatility, while monetarist and New Classical perspectives emphasise monetary discipline in anchoring inflation expectations. Contemporary consensus, however, has shifted the analytical focus toward the *policy mix*: the strategic interaction, sequencing and coordination of the two instruments.

Cameroon, the largest economy in the Central African Economic and Monetary Community (CEMAC), offers a particularly instructive case for examining this interaction. Over the past three decades the country has passed through a succession of distinct macroeconomic regimes. The period opened with the severe crisis of the late 1980s, triggered by collapsing oil and agricultural commodity prices, which exposed the structural fragility of an economy heavily dependent on a narrow export base. The crisis culminated in the January 1994 devaluation of the CFA franc by 50 percent, accompanied by IMF-supported structural adjustment programmes (SAPs). The devaluation restored external competitiveness and marked a watershed in the country's macroeconomic history. It was followed in the 2000s by debt relief under the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) initiative and the Multilateral Debt Relief Initiative (MDRI), which ostensibly restored fiscal space, and by a series of national development strategies—the Growth and Employment Strategy Paper (DSCE, 2010–2020) and the National Development Strategy (NDS30, 2020–2030)—oriented toward the Vision 2035 goal of emergence.

The policy environment has been further shaped by the institutional architecture of the CFA franc zone. Monetary policy for Cameroon is conducted supranationally by the Bank of Central African States (BEAC), under a fixed exchange rate pegged to the euro and backed by the French Treasury's convertibility guarantee through the operations account. In terms of the Mundell–Fleming framework, a fixed exchange rate with open capital mobility implies a surrender of national monetary autonomy. BEAC's mandate is oriented primarily toward price stability and the external coverage of the currency, while fiscal policy remains a sovereign national instrument wielded by the Ministry of Finance (MINFI) and the Ministry of Economy, Planning and Regional Development (MINEPAT). The burden of stabilisation and development financing therefore falls disproportionately on fiscal policy—yet Cameroon's fiscal position has been characterised by persistent structural deficits, weak non-oil revenue mobilisation, rising public debt and procyclical spending tied to volatile commodity prices.

Superimposed on these structural features have been repeated shocks: the 2008–09 global financial crisis, the 2014 collapse in oil prices, the security crisis associated with Boko Haram in the Far North, the socio-political crisis in the Anglophone regions, the COVID-19 pandemic, and the spillovers from the Russia–Ukraine conflict. Each has tested the capacity of the fiscal-monetary mix to absorb shocks without derailing the longer-term development trajectory. Understanding how the combination of these policy tools has facilitated or constrained Cameroon's economic development is therefore not merely an academic question; it is central to informing the next phase of the country's policy strategy.

## 1.2 Problem Statement

Despite three decades of varied fiscal and monetary interventions, Cameroon's development trajectory remains marked by sluggish structural transformation, persistent poverty, high youth unemployment and continued vulnerability to external shocks. Growth has averaged roughly 3.5 to 4.5 percent over the period—rates widely judged insufficient to achieve structural transformation or substantially reduce poverty. A central puzzle emerges from the institutional configuration described above: when the national government adopts an expansionary fiscal stance to finance development, how does this interact with a supranational monetary policy that may be compelled into a restrictive posture to defend reserves or contain imported inflation? Does the Cameroonian framework exhibit fiscal dominance, monetary dominance, or a shifting balance between the two?

Existing scholarship has largely examined fiscal policy and monetary policy in Cameroon in isolation. What is lacking is a comprehensive, longitudinal synthesis that treats the two as an interacting system and traces their combined effects on development outcomes over the full three-decade period. The effectiveness of the 1994 devaluation, the post-HIPC fiscal space, and the NDS30 investment programme cannot be fully understood without reference to the concurrent and often conflicting stances of fiscal and monetary policy. This thesis addresses that gap by asking: **to what extent, and through what mechanisms, have combined fiscal and monetary policies shaped Cameroon's economic development over the past three decades?**

## 1.3 Research Questions

The study is guided by the following primary question:

- **Primary question:** How has the interaction between national fiscal policy and supranational monetary policy shaped Cameroon's economic development over the past three decades?

This is broken down into the following sub-questions:

1. What does the theoretical and empirical literature reveal about fiscal-monetary policy interaction and the policy mix in developing economies and regional monetary unions?
2. How have BEAC's monetary policy regimes and Cameroon's fiscal policy stances evolved in response to major macroeconomic shocks between 1994 and 2024, and what instruments were used?
3. To what extent has the Cameroonian framework been characterised by fiscal dominance versus monetary dominance, and through what channels have the two policies reinforced or conflicted with one another?
4. How has the combined policy mix affected key development indicators—real GDP growth, inflation, public debt sustainability, investment and structural transformation?

## 1.4 Objectives of the Study

The overarching objective is to critically explore the existing literature and analyse the collective impact of fiscal and monetary policies on Cameroon's economic development over the last thirty years. The specific objectives are:

1. To review and synthesise the theoretical and empirical literature on the fiscal-monetary policy mix, with particular emphasis on the CEMAC regional framework.
2. To periodise and characterise the fiscal and monetary policy stances adopted by the Cameroonian government and BEAC from the 1994 devaluation to the post-pandemic period.
3. To assess the relationship, synchronisation and potential conflicts between national fiscal policy and regional monetary policy in Cameroon.
4. To evaluate the developmental outcomes attributable to the combined policy environment and to propose recommendations for enhanced policy coordination in support of Cameroon's structural transformation and emergence goals.

## 1.5 Significance of the Study

**Academically**, the study contributes to the still-thin literature on fiscal-monetary policy coordination in the CEMAC region. By treating Cameroon as a case of sovereign fiscal policy operating without national monetary sovereignty, it enriches the broader debate on policy coordination in monetary unions among asymmetric developing economies, and it bridges historical-qualitative documentation with quantitative econometric work through a long-run synthesis.

**For policymakers**, the findings offer evidence-based insight into the successes and failures of past policy mixes, with direct relevance to MINFI, MINEPAT and BEAC as Cameroon implements NDS30. Understanding the historical trade-offs between domestic revenue mobilisation, regional monetary stringency and public investment is essential for designing resilient, growth-enhancing policy.

**For development partners** such as the IMF, World Bank and African Development Bank, the study provides a critical retrospective on the outcomes of adjustment programmes, debt relief and policy conditionality in the Cameroonian context. **For civil society**, it fosters a clearer understanding of the macroeconomic forces shaping living standards and of the constraints under which national authorities operate.

## 1.6 Scope and Delimitation

The study is geographically delimited to Cameroon, though it is necessarily framed within the CEMAC institutional architecture, since monetary policy is set at the regional level. The temporal scope is the period from 1994 to 2024. The year 1994 is selected as the starting point because the CFA franc devaluation constitutes a structural break that fundamentally altered the macroeconomic landscape and inaugurated the reform era under examination. The analysis focuses on the principal fiscal instruments (government expenditure, taxation and public debt) and monetary instruments (policy rates, money supply and reserve requirements), while acknowledging the constraints imposed by the fixed exchange rate regime.

The principal limitations concern data. Macroeconomic time series for Cameroon are subject to structural breaks, base-year revisions and inconsistencies between national sources (notably the Institut National de la Statistique) and international databases. In addition, because BEAC's decisions are taken for the entire CEMAC zone, disentangling the precise national impact of supranational monetary decisions from that of national fiscal choices presents methodological difficulties that the study must address explicitly.

## 1.7 Organisation of the Thesis

The thesis is organised into five chapters. **Chapter 1** provides the introduction, including background, problem statement, research questions, objectives, significance and scope. **Chapter 2** presents the literature review, examining theoretical foundations—Keynesian, monetarist and the fiscal theory of the price level—and synthesising empirical work on fiscal-monetary interaction in Africa and in monetary unions. **Chapter 3** sets out the institutional and macroeconomic context of Cameroon from 1994 to 2024, tracing policy milestones and major shocks. **Chapter 4** presents the methodology and the empirical analysis, discussing how the policy mix has shaped development outcomes. **Chapter 5** concludes with a summary of findings, policy recommendations and avenues for further research.

The Spanish presidency of the EU Council has circulated a first draft legal text setting out obligations for foundation models and General Purpose AI (GPAI) in the AI Act, as negotiations enter their final trilogue phase between the Council, Parliament and Commission. The text follows the tiered approach EU policymakers have been converging on since ChatGPT's rise, with stricter rules for the most powerful models.

**Foundation models** are defined as large AI models trained on large amounts of data that can competently perform a wide range of distinct tasks (e.g. generating video, text, images or code, conversing in natural language, computing). Their providers must:
- Give AI system providers up-to-date technical documentation on the model's capacities and limitations, plus elements detailed in an annex.
- Show they took adequate measures so training complied with EU copyright law, in particular the rule that text and data mining of publicly available online content requires rightsholders' consent, including by machine-readable means, where rightsholders have opted out of the mining exception. Developers must therefore put in place a system to respect creators' opt-outs.
- Publish a sufficiently detailed summary of the training content and of how copyright-related aspects are managed, based on a Commission template.

**High-impact foundation models** — defined as foundation models trained on large amounts of data with complexity, capabilities and performance well above the average for foundation models, able to spread systemic risks along the value chain whether or not integrated into a high-risk system — face a stricter regime. Within 18 months of the law's entry into force, the Commission must adopt implementing or delegated acts setting the classification thresholds in line with market and technological developments, and will designate the models meeting them in consultation with the AI Office. Obligations include:
- Adversarial vetting (red-teaming); still under discussion is how this applies to models commercialised as a system integrating components such as traditional software, as with GPT-4, and whether external experts must do the testing — the presidency considers the provider can, since these models will also be audited.
- The AI Office may request documentation proving compliance and, on reasoned request, mandate an independent audit of compliance with the law and with commitments under codes of conduct the Commission should encourage.
- A "possibly additional" obligation to set up a system for tracking serious incidents and corrective measures.
- At least yearly systemic risk assessments in the EU, from market launch and for each new version, including risks from integration into an AI system, covering dissemination of illegal or harmful content and reasonably foreseeable negative effects such as major accidents or impacts on democratic processes.

The Commission would be empowered to adjust these provisions as market and technology evolve, and the law's chapeau provisions would clarify what an AI model is, how it is built, the interaction between datasets and foundation models, and how applications are built on top of them.

**General Purpose AI systems** — such as ChatGPT, defined as systems that may be based on an AI model, can include additional components like traditional software, and through a user interface can serve a variety of purposes, both directly and when integrated into other AI systems — would face obligations when providers enter licensing agreements with downstream operators that may use the system for one or more high-risk use cases. Providers must state in the instructions the high-risk uses for which the system may be used and supply technical documentation and all information the downstream provider needs to meet high-risk requirements. They may also prohibit certain high-risk uses, in which case they must take all necessary and proportionate measures to detect and enforce against misuse.

# Prologue: The Ghosts of the Armory

The Bedford-Stuyvesant Armory in Brooklyn has stood for a century—its brick walls soaked with sweat, liniment, and ambition. Long before it became the home of the New York Women's Combat Roster (NYWCR), it was a boxing gym, a roller rink, a shelter. Now it houses the most storied promotion in women's fighting, and its Hall of Champions is lined with brass plaques. One name glows brighter than the rest: **Rosa "La Reina" Jiménez**, the roster's first great champion, whose granddaughter would one day rule the same ring. And beside her, two names that still feel like a scar: **Jasmine Jiménez** and **Hilda Rosario**.

An aging custodian polishes the plaques and mutters to himself: *"The fire and the flood. They burned this place down and rebuilt it a dozen times."* Above him hangs a torn, faded poster—two women, faces inches apart, eyes blazing. He turns off the light and leaves the ghosts in the dark.

---

# The Reason for Fighting

**For Jasmine:** The NYWCR is her birthright. Her grandmother, Rosa, was its first and most beloved champion, and Jasmine grew up in the gym learning every hold and secret from the woman she idolized. The title is a sacred trust, and the roster is her family's kingdom. To her, Hilda is a flashy outsider who doesn't understand the history or the sacrifice.

**For Hilda:** Hilda comes from nothing—Washington Heights, the daughter of a Dominican immigrant who worked three jobs. Fighting is her way out, her art, and her chance to write her own name into history rather than inherit it. Her easy-going confidence reads as arrogance to the old guard. To her, Jasmine is a gatekeeper protecting a throne she was born onto.

The title is only the symbol. What they are really fighting over is respect, legacy, and the question neither can answer alone: *who is the best?*

---

# Part I: The Ascent (Chapters 1–15)

1. **The Streak** — Hilda Rosario, a relative unknown, demolishes local opponents with unorthodox, rhythm-based technique. Her manager, savvy veteran Mickey Doyle, sees dollar signs.
2. **The Rival** — Hilda's tenth win comes against Karen, a tough Colombian brunette and Jasmine's long-time rival and #1 contender. Hilda wins via a shocking acrobatic submission.
3. **The Pitch** — Mickey uses the Karen win to get Hilda a meeting with NYWCR manager Eleanor Vance, a stern, calculating promoter.
4. **The Roster** — Hilda signs. On her first day at the Armory she walks in with a confident swagger; Jasmine, the reigning champion, watches from across the gym, unimpressed.
5. **First Encounter** — Jasmine "welcomes" Hilda by belittling her in front of the whole roster: *"A win streak against bums doesn't mean anything here, chica. This is the big leagues."*
6. **The Retort** — Hilda fires back without missing a beat: *"And beating Karen, who you couldn't put away for two years, does. Good to know."* The room goes silent. The rivalry is born.
7. **Tension Builds** — Forced to share the gym, every workout becomes a silent competition. Jasmine critiques Hilda's form; Hilda mocks Jasmine's old-school methods.
8. **The Cold War** — They're booked in tag matches with different partners, each trying to outshine the other.
9. **The First Skirmish** — A backstage argument over a scheduling conflict escalates into a brief, intense scuffle of shoves and holds before being pulled apart. The line has been crossed.
10. **Hilda's Momentum** — Hilda keeps winning, her popularity soaring. She's flashy, charismatic, and connects with a new generation of fans.

# Video Presentation: Singapore English — Speaking Englishes in Global Contexts

**Format note:** This is a complete script plus slide plan for a 10–15 minute video presentation. Each slide lists bullet content and a spoken narration you can deliver on camera. Every example can be demonstrated aloud — essential for an orthoepy presentation.

---

## Slide 1 — Title

**Singapore English: The Sound of a Global City**
*Orthoepy: Speaking Englishes in Global Contexts*

**Opening narration:**
"Have you ever heard 'Can lah!' and understood it completely — or been completely lost? That gap between intelligibility and identity is what Singapore English is all about. Today I'll show you how a variety of English shaped by Hokkien, Malay, Tamil and Mandarin has its own systematic vocabulary, pronunciation, grammar and expressions — and why it matters for global communication."

---

## Slide 2 — What Is Singapore English?

- **Singapore English** = the English of Singapore (~6 million people), the nation's first language and medium of education, government, law and business.
- It exists on a **continuum**:
  - **Standard Singapore English (SSE)** — formal, internationally intelligible; news, parliament, academia.
  - **Colloquial Singapore English (CSE, "Singlish")** — the informal, creole-like variety of everyday speech.
- Substrate languages: **Hokkien, Teochew, Cantonese, Mandarin, Malay, Tamil**.
- It is **rule-governed, not "bad English."**

**Narration:** "The key framing: Singapore English sits where the postcolonial British legacy meets Asian multilingual identity. On the continuum, educated speakers move fluidly between a formal standard and a colloquial variety — a diglossic situation linguists like Gupta have described."

---

## Slide 3 — Unique Vocabulary

**Borrowings from Chinese varieties (mainly Hokkien):**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **kiasu** | fear of losing out; ultra-competitive (*kia* = afraid, *su* = lose) |
| **kiasi** | "afraid to die"; overly cautious |
| **paiseh** | embarrassed / shy |
| **sian** | bored, fed up |
| **wah lau** | expression of dismay or surprise |
| **ang moh** | a Caucasian (literally "red-haired") |
| **bo chap** | indifferent, couldn't care less |
| **tapao / dabao** | takeaway food (via Cantonese) |

**Borrowings from Malay:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **makan** | to eat / food |
| **shiok** | fantastic, deeply satisfying |
| **alamak** | "oh no!" |
| **kena** | to be subjected to (usually something bad — *kena scolding*) |
| **lepak** | to loiter, relax |
| **sabo** | to sabotage / prank someone |

**Borrowings from Tamil:** **goondu** (fool, idiot); **machan** (buddy).

**English words with localized meanings:**
- **blur** = confused, slow to catch on ("He very blur one")
- **follow** = understand ("You follow?")
- **send** = take someone somewhere ("I send you home")
- **stay** = live ("I stay in Tampines")
- **open / off** = turn on / turn off ("Open the light"; "Off the fan, can?")

**Narration:** "Notice the lexical *export*: *kiasu* was added to the Oxford English Dictionary in 2015, and words like *shiok*, *makan* and *chope* circulate well beyond Singapore."

---

## Slide 4 — Unique Pronunciation (the orthoepy core)

**Consonants:**
- **Final consonant cluster reduction:** *text* → "tex", *asked* → "ask", *fact* → "fack" (often with a glottal stop).
- **/θ/ and /ð/ → /t/ and /d/:** *three* → "tree", *this* → "dis", *brother* → "broder".
- **Final /l/ vocalization:** *milk* → [mɪʊk], *cool* → "coo".

**Vowels:**
- **Monophthongization of diphthongs:** *go* → [goː], *take* → [teːk], *face* → [feːs].
- **Reduced vowel contrasts:** tense/lax pairs like *sheep*/*ship* and *pool*/*pull* can converge; the overall vowel space is smaller than RP or General American.

**Prosody (most distinctive):**
- **Syllable-timed rhythm** rather than stress-timed — each syllable gets roughly equal weight, influenced by Sinitic and Malay rhythm.
- **Different stress placement** in some words, and **less vowel reduction** in unstressed syllables — full vowels where RP would use schwa.
- **Distinctive intonation**, including rising contours on some statements; outsiders may misread this as uncertainty, but it functions as a marker of local identity.

**Narration:** "These are not random errors — they are systematic, predictable patterns, which is exactly what orthoepy studies. Compare the stress-timed 'I'm going to the SU-per-mar-ket' with the more even 'I go su-per-mar-ket.'"

> **Caution for the presenter:** Don't overstate any single feature as universal. Singapore English is a continuum, and the precise vowel qualities and intonation patterns are documented with acoustic detail in David Deterding's research — cite him rather than asserting absolute rules.

---

## Slide 5 — Unique Grammar

**1. Topic-comment structure (from Chinese):**
- "This book, I already read." / "That movie, very nice."

**2. Optional tense marking; context carries time:**
- "Yesterday I go market."

**3. Reduplication:**
- Verbal: "He walk walk walk" (walking continuously); "see-see" (take a look).
- Adjectival: "nice nice," "big big" (intensity).

**4. Aspect particles:**
- **already** = perfective: "I eat already."
- **got** = existential / possessive: "Got money or not?"; "I got see him."
- **still** = continuative: "He still sleeping."

**5. Copula deletion:**
- "He very smart." / "She my sister."

**6. Questions without inversion:**
- A-not-A pattern: "You want go or not?" / "Can or not?"
- Invariant tags: "You going, is it?"

**7. Variable plurals and articles:**
- "I bought two book." / "He is teacher."

**8. "One" as nominalizer/emphatic:** "That one very expensive one." / "He blur one."

**9. Discourse particles (the signature of Singlish):**

| Particle | Function | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **lah** | solidarity, emphasis, softening | "Come lah!" |
| **lor** | resignation, obviousness | "Like that lor." |
| **leh** | mild assertion / query | "Why you so late leh?" |
| **meh** | skepticism | "Really meh?" |
| **sia** | strong emphasis (Malay origin) | "Wah, shiok sia!" |
| **hor** | seeking agreement | "Not bad hor?" |
| **mah** | justification | "I tired mah." |

**Narration:** "The particles are the heart of it. They carry pragmatic meaning — stance, politeness, solidarity. Remove them and you change the social meaning, not just the style."

---

## Slide 6 — Unique Expressions & Idioms

- **"Can lah!"** — the all-purpose Singaporean yes (*can*, *can lah*, *can can*, *cannot*).
- **"Don't play play."** — Don't mess around / don't underestimate.
- **"Wait long long."** — Don't hold your breath (sarcastic).
- **"Go where?"** — Where are you going?
- **"What you talking?"** — What are you talking about?
- **"So how?"** — What now? / How's it going?
- **"Chope"** — reserve a seat, famously with a tissue packet.
- **"Catch no ball"** — not understand at all (calque of a Hokkien expression).
- **"Shiok!"** — deep satisfaction.
- **"My English very powderful."** — self-deprecating joke on "powerful."

**Narration:** "Humor and irony are central — Singlish is a playful, creative register. The 'powderful' joke shows metalinguistic awareness: Singaporeans know exactly when they're code-switching."

---

## Slide 7 — The Continuum and Code-Switching

- Formal: "I would like to request a meeting with the manager."
- Colloquial: "Eh, can meet your boss or not?"
- **Domain-based switching:** Standard English in school, parliament, news; Singlish with friends, family, at hawker centres.
- The **Speak Good English Movement (launched 2000)** explicitly targets Singlish — yet Singlish thrives, showing its **identity function**.
- **Core orthoepic insight:** Singapore English is a self-contained system — *variety, not deficiency*.

---

## Slide 8 — Impact on Global Communication

**1. Intelligibility:** Research on World Englishes (Deterding, Kirkpatrick) indicates **Standard Singapore English is highly intelligible** internationally, while heavy Singlish is less so to outsiders — yet fully intelligible within the community. Intelligibility is **graded and context-dependent**, not absolute.

**2. Singapore as a model of English as a Lingua Franca:** The bilingual policy (English + mother tongue) produced a highly proficient, globally mobile workforce. Singapore English is increasingly exported through media (e.g., *Crazy Rich Asians*, Singaporean content creators) and through Singaporeans in international business.

**3. Lexical and cultural export:** *Kiasu*, *shiok*, *chope* and hawker culture (UNESCO-listed) circulate in global media and dictionaries; *kiasu* has become a globally recognized label for competitive culture.

**4. The central tension:** The government worries Singlish harms international competitiveness; linguists and citizens argue it builds national identity and cohesion. This is the classic World Englishes debate: **standardization vs. pluralism**.

**5. Lessons:** English is **pluricentric** — no single "correct" orthoepy. Singapore English models **pragmatic competence**: code-switching to stay globally intelligible while keeping a local voice. **Accommodation** — adjusting toward your interlocutor — is the key skill, and Singaporeans practice it daily.

---

## Slide 9 — Conclusion

- A **laboratory of language contact**: Chinese, Malay, Tamil and English fused into a living system.
- Its vocabulary, pronunciation, grammar and particles are **systematic, creative and identity-bearing** — not errors.
- It shows that **orthoepy must be descriptive, not prescriptive**: the study of "correct" pronunciation must account for global varieties.
- **Intelligibility and identity can coexist** — through code-switching, accommodation and mutual respect.

**Closing line:** "Singlish is not English gone wrong — it is English gone *local*, and in a globalized world, 'local' is where meaning lives."

---

## Slide 10 — References & Further Reading

- Deterding, D. (2007). *Singapore English*. Edinburgh University Press.
- Lim, L. (ed.) (2004). *Singapore English: A Grammatical Description*. John Benjamins.
- Platt, J. & Weber, H. (1980). *English in Singapore and Malaysia*.
- Tongue, R. K. (1979). *The English of Singapore and Malaysia*.
- Pakir, A. (1991). "The range and depth of English-knowing bilinguals in Singapore." *World Englishes*.
- Gupta, A. F. (1994). *The Step-Tongue: Children's English in Singapore*.
- Kirkpatrick, A. (2010). *World Englishes: Implications for International Communication and English Language Teaching*.
- Oxford English Dictionary — entries for *kiasu*, *lah*.
- Speak Good English Movement official materials (for the prescriptivist counterpoint).

ρ ≈ 8190 kg/m³, E ≈ 200 GPa, ν ≈ 0.29, σy ≈ 1030 MPa, σUTS ≈ 1280 MPa. For crash use, add a rate-dependent or Johnson–Cook plasticity table as well.

---

## 3. Modelling notes for crashworthiness in Abaqus/Explicit

1. **Solver:** Abaqus/Explicit for impact, contact and blade release; the implicit solver struggles with Hashin softening and element deletion.
2. **Units:** stay in one consistent system (mm–tonne–s–N–MPa is the standard for crash models).
3. **Elements:** C3D8R with **enhanced hourglass control** for solids; SC8R or S4R for composite shells; watch out for hourglass energy.
4. **Contact:** general contact (Explicit) with penalty stiffness; include self-contact for fragmentation and blade containment.
5. **Energy checks:** keep artificial strain energy and hourglass energy below ~5 % of internal energy; use mass scaling only selectively and verify kinetic energy stays small relative to internal energy.
6. **Composite mesh sensitivity:** Hashin + energy evolution results depend strongly on element size — run a mesh convergence check on at least one blade/casing coupon before the full model.

# Deceased Estates and Maintenance under ASX Requirements – An Orientation

This is educational background, not legal or compliance advice. The operative sources are the **ASX Settlement Operating Rules (ASX SO Rules)** (with the ASX Clear Operating Rules where relevant), the **ASX CHESS user guides and participant technical specifications**, and your own participant's procedures. Always confirm against the current rulebook and ASX guidance, and note that much of the estate paperwork (probate, resealing of foreign grants) is governed by state/territory law and registry practice, not by ASX rules directly.

## Background

- **CHESS** holds uncertificated holdings against **HINs** (Holder Identification Numbers). A **participant** (broker) sponsors the HIN; an **issuer's registry** may also hold issuer-sponsored holdings.
- ASX rules govern how the **participant** interacts with CHESS: what it may request, what controls apply, and when a HIN can be cancelled or a holding transmitted.
- Three concepts recur: **survivorship** (joint holdings passing to the survivor outside the estate), **transmission** (transfer of a deceased holder's securities to the executor/administrator or beneficiaries), and **HIN locks** (freezing a HIN while authority is established).

---

## a) Survivorship requests

**What it is:** Where holders are **joint tenants**, on the death of one the holding passes automatically to the surviving joint holder(s). It does not form part of the deceased estate and does not pass under the Will.

**In practice:**
- The surviving holder (or their participant) asks for the deceased holder's name to be removed and the holding re-registered in the survivor's name.
- Typically requires a **certified death certificate**, identification of the survivor, and a survivorship/transmission request form (registry- or participant-specific). A grant of probate is normally **not** required for a pure joint-tenancy survivorship.
- The participant must be satisfied of the death and of the joint tenancy before acting, and should keep that evidence on file.

**Watch-outs:**
- **Joint tenants vs tenants in common.** Tenants in common do **not** get survivorship; the deceased's share falls into the estate and needs probate/letters of administration.
- Check whether the holding is **CHESS-sponsored** (participant handles it) or **issuer-sponsored** (registry handles it).
- The exact CHESS mechanics of re-registering a joint holding (amending registration details versus establishing a new HIN for the survivor and transferring the securities, then closing the old HIN) vary with the circumstances and the participant's procedures; confirm the current CHESS process before you rely on one route.

---

## b) Deceased and non-deceased estate HIN locks and unlocks

**Purpose:** A HIN lock restricts dealings on a HIN (for example, transfers out or trading) while authority is being established. It protects the estate and the participant from liability. A lock is a **risk-control overlay** — it does not change legal ownership. Locks may be internal participant/registry controls, and CHESS also supports lock functions; use whichever mechanism your procedures and ASX guidance require.

**Deceased estate lock:**
- Applied when the participant is notified of a holder's death, to freeze the HIN pending estate documents (probate or letters of administration, transmission forms).
- Open orders should be dealt with promptly, and no dealings permitted until authority is verified.
- Released, or the holding transmitted, once the executor's/administrator's authority is verified and instructions are received from the authorised legal personal representative. Often the HIN is not simply reopened for ordinary trading; it may be unlocked only to allow transmission to an estate HIN or to beneficiaries, after which the original HIN is closed.

**Non-deceased ("administrative") lock:**
- A lock placed for reasons other than the holder's death — for example, disputed authority, fraud concerns, court orders, bankruptcy, failed settlement, or regulatory/sanctions flags. It can also apply where an estate is being administered but the registered holder is still living (e.g. a power-of-attorney dispute).
- **Unlock** requires resolution of the underlying trigger and written instruction from the authorised party, with identity and authority verified (probate, letters of administration, court order, POA) and the participant's internal sign-off and audit trail.

---

## c) HIN cancellation requests

A HIN generally cannot be cancelled while it holds assets or has pending activity.

**Pre-conditions:**
1. **Nil balance** — all securities transferred out (off-market transfer, conversion to issuer sponsorship, or sale and settlement).
2. **No pending activity** — no outstanding settlements, pending corporate actions, or unclaimed entitlements.
3. **No active locks** — locks must be removed first.

**Deceased-estate context:** Once the holding has been transmitted to the executor/administrator or distributed to beneficiaries (or sold), the deceased holder's HIN is typically cancelled as the final administrative step.

**ASX angle:** The ASX SO Rules prescribe the HIN lifecycle (establishment, amendment, cancellation) and the participant's obligation to keep CHESS records accurate. Cancellation must be properly authorised and recorded. The precise CHESS message flow for cancellation is set out in the CHESS participant specifications — check the current version rather than relying on remembered message numbers.

---

## d) Deceased international account suspensions

Where a client held **international securities** (e.g. US or UK shares) through a broker's omnibus or custodian arrangement, the process differs from CHESS because the assets sit with a foreign custodian and foreign law applies.

**Why suspend:** The account (and any related HIN) is suspended on notification of death so that nothing is dealt with before the foreign personal representative's authority is recognised. Cross-border estates raise harder issues: foreign probate requirements, tax (including US estate-tax exposure on US-situs assets above the relevant threshold and the IRS transfer-certificate process), withholding and FATCA/CRS reporting, and AML/KYC verification of foreign executors.

**Process (general):**
- Place the suspension/HIN lock on notification of death.
- Collect a **certified foreign death certificate**, the **grant of probate/letters of administration** (often with an **apostille** or consular legalisation), certified **translations** where needed, and ID of the foreign executor.
- Depending on the jurisdiction, the foreign grant may need to be **resealed** in the relevant Australian state or territory, or local legal advice obtained.
- Once the custodian's legal/compliance function is satisfied (including any foreign tax clearance), the suspension is lifted and the holdings transmitted or realised, with proceeds repatriated.

**ASX angle:** ASX rules do not prescribe foreign probate law, but they require the participant to act only on properly evidenced authority and to maintain records. The suspension is the participant's control while that authority is established.

---

## Practical checklist

1. **Identify the holding type** — joint tenancy vs tenants in common; CHESS-sponsored vs issuer-sponsored; domestic vs international.
2. **Confirm the death** — certified death certificate, and note the date of death (it affects entitlements).
3. **Apply the right control** — survivorship request, deceased-estate HIN lock, international account suspension, or non-deceased lock.
4. **Obtain authority documents** — probate/letters of administration, survivorship form, foreign grant with apostille/reseal as needed.
5. **Lodge the CHESS/registry instruction** — transmission, cancellation, or unlock — with a full audit trail.
6. **Reconcile entitlements** — dividends, corporate actions, and tax — before closing the HIN.
7. **Document everything** — ASX expects participants to be able to evidence the basis for every lock, unlock, cancellation, and transmission.

## Where to go for the authoritative detail

- **ASX Settlement Operating Rules** (HIN, transmission, and participant-obligation provisions) and **ASX Clear Operating Rules**.
- **ASX CHESS user guides and participant technical specifications** on transmission, locks, and HIN maintenance.
- Your **registry's deceased-estate procedure** (e.g. Computershare or Link Market Services forms), which operationalises the ASX rules.
- **ASIC** guidance on deceased estates, and state/territory probate authorities for resealing foreign grants.

If you tell me which part you'll be handling first — for example the CHESS transmission workflow, or foreign probate/reseal for a particular jurisdiction — I can go deeper on that.

# Incorporating Higher-Than-Expected Claims Inflation into Reserves

The core problem is that standard reserving methods (chain ladder, Bornhuetter–Ferguson, etc.) implicitly assume that the inflation embedded in historical development patterns will continue. If future inflation departs from the past—especially a surge driven by demand and supply-side shocks—those methods will understate ultimate costs, and the effect is amplified for long-tail business where inflation compounds over many years.

## Part 1: Methods available

**1. Deflation / reflation (constant-dollar) approach.** Strip historical inflation out of the paid and incurred triangles using an appropriate index, so the triangle is expressed in constant cost terms. Apply the standard projection to the deflated data, then reflate the projected future cash flows using an explicit, higher future inflation assumption. This is the most economically coherent approach and directly addresses distortion in historical development factors.

**2. Explicit adjustment to the inflation assumption in the model.** Replace the base inflation assumption with an elevated one (or a path) and re-run the projection. Variants include a fixed point uplift, a phased/ramped assumption (elevated for a period, reverting to long-run levels—appropriate if the surge is seen as temporary), or a set of scenarios with the booked estimate set at a chosen point in the range.

**3. Calendar-year / separation methods.** Because inflation is a calendar-year effect (it affects all claims paid in a given year regardless of accident year), models that explicitly estimate accident-year, development-year and calendar-year parameters (Taylor/Verbeek separation, GLM frameworks with a calendar-year term, Munich chain ladder variants) let the actuary overwrite the future calendar-year parameter with an explicit inflation forecast, separating genuine development from inflationary distortion.

**4. Frequency–severity modelling.** Model counts and average costs separately, with inflation applied explicitly to severity (allowing for settlement lags) and different assumptions by cost driver. Useful where inflation mainly hits severity (repair, medical, wages) rather than frequency.

**5. Adjustments to standard selections.** Shorten the averaging period for development factors to weight recent experience more heavily, increase tail factors, or raise the a priori loss ratio (ELR) in Bornhuetter–Ferguson/Cape Cod where recent accident years have not yet fully reflected the new inflation.

**6. Case reserve re-estimation.** For long-tail lines and large claims, re-price outstanding claims at current cost levels (updated repair estimates, medical cost projections). This corrects known inadequacy in case reserves directly.

**7. Judgmental overlay / margin.** Apply a documented loading on top of the model output, calibrated to sensitivity analysis (e.g. the change in reserves for +1%, +2% inflation). Simple and easy to communicate, but can be arbitrary without supporting analysis and risks double-counting if other adjustments are also made.

**8. Sensitivity testing and scenario/stress analysis.** Quantify reserves across a range of inflation assumptions and scenarios (transient vs persistent; demand-pull vs supply-shock). This may not change the central estimate but informs the margin/risk adjustment, disclosures, and ORSA/capital work.

**9. Stochastic inflation modelling.** Embed inflation as a stochastic variable (linked to CPI/interest rate models or an AR process with regime shifts) in a stochastic reserving framework, producing a distribution of reserves that feeds the risk margin and capital model.

**10. Claims-specific indices.** Rather than headline CPI, use indices matched to the portfolio—construction costs, used car parts, medical inflation, wage inflation, court award trends (social inflation)—possibly blended with the insurer's own experience. This is usually a refinement of methods 1 and 2 rather than a standalone method.

## Part 2: Factors in choosing a method

- **Nature and cause of the inflation.** Is the surge transient (supply-chain) or persistent (wage-price)? This determines whether a phased assumption or a permanent uplift is appropriate, and which indices and lines are exposed.
- **Tail length and line of business.** Short-tail lines (property, motor damage) are affected quickly but only over a short horizon, so simpler parameter adjustments may suffice. Long-tail lines (casualty, bodily injury, workers' compensation) face compounding over many years, where explicit deflation/reflation or calendar-year separation is usually necessary.
- **Type of inflation and cost drivers.** Whether exposure is driven by materials, medical costs, wages or litigation/social inflation, and whether policy limits or caps constrain the exposure.
- **Case reserving behaviour.** If claims handlers have already raised case reserves, incurred-based methods may double-count inflation; this needs investigation before adding loadings.
- **Data availability and credibility.** Explicit methods need reliable historical claims indices, consistent settlement/report dates and enough data to separate inflation from development. Where data are scarce or confounded (mix changes, legal environment), a high-level overlay or scenario range may be the only defensible route.
- **Materiality and proportionality.** The sophistication should match the size of the exposure relative to reserves, capital and earnings, and the cost/benefit of the modelling.
- **Model risk and uncertainty.** Simple loadings are transparent but crude; stochastic models are richer but harder to validate and explain. Where confidence in the inflation view is low, a range or sensitivity approach may be preferable to a single point assumption, and prudence typically argues against understating reserves.
- **Consistency with other assumptions.** Discount rates, reinsurance recoveries (including reinsurance bad-debt risk and any caps/aggregates), expenses and investment returns are all affected by inflation and should be set consistently.
- **Accounting and regulatory framework.** Whether the basis is best estimate or prudent, and how the method feeds the risk adjustment/risk margin (IFRS 17, Solvency II, US GAAP), including any prescribed stress tests and sensitivity disclosures.
- **Governance and communication.** Documentation, audit trail and the ability to explain and defend the approach to the board, auditors and regulators; consistency with pricing, capital modelling and ORSA scenarios.

In practice, actuaries usually combine approaches: re-estimate using claims-specific indices and inflation-adjusted development, test sensitivity across scenarios, set the central estimate with an explicit documented assumption plus a judgmental margin where warranted, and disclose the range and stresses. The choice should be proportionate to materiality, supported by data where possible, and fully documented.

The 7:42 from Bakersfield to Northgate was a world in miniature, and I knew every inch of its geography by heart. I had ridden it six days a week for three years, ever since I started at Northgate Technical Academy, and I could have drawn its floor plan blindfolded: the four-car arrangement, the scuffed vinyl of the seats, the faint smell of diesel and orange cleaner that clung to the whole train, and the strange, faintly yellow light that leaked in through the scratched windows on gray mornings like this one.

My name is Daniel Reyes, and I was seventeen, with a lean frame that hadn't quite caught up to my height yet, dark hair that needed cutting, and hands that always seemed to be in motion—turning a screwdriver, stripping a wire, worrying at the seam of my jacket. I carried an olive-drab backpack heavy with the things I trusted: a multimeter, a soldering iron, a spool of solder, a roll of electrical tape, a battered tin of assorted resistors, and a notebook full of half-finished schematics. It was the only thing I owned that felt like an extension of my own head.

The train was crowded that morning. The overhead lights buzzed faintly, and the heater under the seats clicked on and off with a soft, regular tick. In the seat across the aisle, an old man in a herringbone coat was doing the crossword, muttering the clues under his breath. Behind him, two women in scrubs—nurses, by the look of them—talked softly about a patient they'd lost the night before. Near the doors, a boy about my age in a Northgate letterman jacket leaned against the glass with his headphones on, his head bobbing slightly to a beat none of us could hear. His name was on the back of the jacket: *Kowalski*.

I had my own headphones on, but they were dead—the left driver had given up the night before, and I hadn't gotten around to resoldering it. So I sat there, watching the gray city slide past, listening to the low murmur of the carriage and the rhythmic *clack-clack-clack* of the wheels over the joints, and thinking about the circuit I was going to build in third period: a little oscillator that would light an LED in a pattern that traced the Fibonacci sequence. It was the kind of pointless, beautiful thing that made electronics feel like magic.

Then the brakes fired.

There was no warning—no slow deceleration, no polite hiss of the pneumatic system. It was a scream of steel on steel, a sound that seemed to come from the bones of the train itself. The car bucked, and I was thrown forward against the seat in front of me, my shoulder slamming into the hard plastic. My backpack slid off the seat and hit the floor with a heavy clank. The old man's crossword flew from his lap; the nurses grabbed each other; Kowalski's headphones went skittering across the floor.

The train tilted, and for one long, horrible second I thought we were going over. Then the wheels locked and we ground to a halt with a final, shuddering jolt that left the whole car leaning a few degrees to the right, like a ship run aground.

For a moment there was nothing but silence—the deep, ringing silence that comes after a very loud noise—and then the shouting began.

"What the hell was that?"

"Did we hit something?"

"Is everyone okay? Is anyone hurt?"

I got up slowly, my shoulder aching, and retrieved my backpack from the floor. My hands were shaking, but I forced them to be steady as I checked the contents—multimeter intact, soldering iron in its case, notebook still there. I slung it back over my shoulder and looked out the window.

We were stopped just short of a level crossing, maybe two hundred meters before it. The front of the train was off to my left, and through the grimy glass I could see a knot of people gathered on the road beyond the crossing, pointing and talking, their faces pale even at this distance. A car had stopped in the middle of the road with its door open.

And then I saw what they were looking at.

There was a shape on the tracks near the front of the train. A person. A man, from the dark trousers and the way one arm was flung out at an angle that arms weren't supposed to make. The morning light was flat and gray, but it caught the wet sheen of something dark spreading across the gravel between the rails, a slow, ugly stain that seemed to be widening as I watched.

A woman behind me let out a small, high sound, and then I heard someone being sick into a paper bag. The old man crossed himself. Kowalski stood with his face pressed against the glass, his mouth slightly open.

The conductor's voice came over the intercom, crackling with static, strained in a way I had never heard from a train conductor before. "Ladies and gentlemen, please remain calm. We have struck a—there has been an incident on the track ahead. We are in contact with the authorities. Please remain in your seats. Do not attempt to exit the train."

Nobody remained in their seats. The doors hissed open—someone had pulled the emergency release—and people spilled out onto the ballast, a confused, frightened crowd. I didn't follow them. I stood there for another moment, watching, and something cold settled into the pit of my stomach.

The shape on the tracks had moved.

It was small, the way a distant thing is small, and in the confusion I told myself I was mistaken. But I had seen it—a twitch of the arm, a slow, jerking contraction of the fingers against the gravel. The man was dead; you don't survive that, nobody survives that. And yet the fingers moved.

I turned away from the window and walked to the doors.

Outside, the air was cold and sharp, and it smelled of diesel and iron and something else, something sweet and wrong. The crowd had gathered along the side of the train, kept back from the front by the driver, a gray-faced man in a blue uniform who was waving his arms and shouting. "Stay back! Stay back, please! Don't look!"

I looked anyway. I couldn't help it.

The man on the tracks was in pieces. The train had done what trains do to a body, and there was no dignity left in the thing on the gravel. But it was the face that stopped me—turned up toward the sky, the jaw hanging slack, the eyes open. The eyes were wrong. They were milky, clouded, like the eyes of a fish left too long in the sun, and as I watched, they seemed to shift, very slightly, toward the sound of the driver's voice.

I felt my breakfast rise in my throat, and I turned away, stumbling back from the crowd.

Northgate was only a mile and a half away, maybe a twenty-minute walk along the service road that ran beside the tracks. The thought of getting back on that train, of sitting in that carriage with the image of the thing on the tracks still burning behind my eyes, was unbearable. I needed to move. I needed the cold air to clear my head.

I walked.

The service road was empty at first, and the only sounds were the distant sirens and the crunch of my boots on the gravel. The city was waking up around me, oblivious—cars on the highway, a dog barking somewhere, the low rumble of a truck downshifting. The ordinary world, going about its ordinary business, while behind me a crowd stood around a dead man on the tracks.

I had gone about a hundred meters when I saw the first runner.

He came around the corner of a warehouse at a full sprint, a man in a tracksuit, and he didn't slow down when he saw me. He didn't even look at me. His face was a mask of pure, animal terror, his mouth open, his breath coming in ragged gasps. He pounded past me, his footsteps echoing off the corrugated metal of the warehouse wall, and vanished around the next corner.

A moment later, a woman in a business suit came running after him, her heels clacking frantically on the pavement, her handbag bouncing against her hip. Then another man, and another. Then a whole crowd of them, pouring out of the side streets, a river of panicked humanity flowing away from the city center.

The screams started a moment later.

I stopped in the middle of the road, my heart hammering. The sound was rising from ahead of me, from the direction of the school, a chorus of screams and shouts and something else, something underneath it all, a low, guttural chorus that didn't sound like anything I had ever heard.

I should have turned back. Any sane person would have turned back. But Northgate was ahead, and the school was a fortress of concrete and steel, and my feet were already moving.

I rounded the corner onto Merchant Avenue, and the horror confronted me.

Merchant Avenue was a wide, tree-lined street, four lanes of traffic that ran past the school's eastern boundary. On a normal morning it was busy but orderly, cars streaming toward the city center, students walking along the sidewalks. Now it was a slaughterhouse.

Cars were stopped at crazy angles, some with their doors hanging open, others smashed into the lampposts or the trees. A bus had jumped the curb and was sitting half on the sidewalk, its front end crumpled. And among the cars, moving in the gray morning light, were the things.

I saw one clearly, thirty meters away: a man in a postal uniform, his blue shirt shredded and dark with something wet, his skin the color of old candle wax. His head was cocked to one side at an impossible angle, and he was walking—no, shambling—with a slow, jerking gait, his arms hanging loose at his sides. His eyes were milky white, unfocused, dead. And yet he was moving, his head turning slowly from side to side, his nose twitching at the air.

He was sniffing.

A woman lay on the ground a few meters from him, and another of the things—a woman in a floral dress, her hair a tangled mess—was crouched over her, her head jerking back and forth with a horrible, mechanical rhythm. I heard the wet, tearing sound of it, and I looked away.

A security guard stumbled into the street, blood streaming from a wound on his arm, and one of the creatures—a woman in a tattered business suit—went after him. She moved with a jerky, uncoordinated gait, but she was fast, faster than she had any right to be. She caught him before he made it ten meters, and her teeth sank into his neck, and his scream was a wet, gurgling thing that cut off abruptly.

I stood frozen, my backpack a lead weight on my shoulders, my mind screaming in protest. This was impossible. This was a hallucination, a fever dream, something out of a movie. But the smell of copper was thick in the air, and the screams were real, and the blood on the pavement was real.

And then one of them turned toward me.

It was a gaunt man with a huge, blood-soaked beard, his clothes hanging off him in rags. He was twenty meters away, and he was staring in my direction—but not at me, I realized.
