# Alternate Ending: "Go Goo Go" — and Beyond

## The New Ending

In the original episode, Mac's apology fixes things and Goo goes back to being a friend who only visits on special occasions. Here's where it changes:

After Mac's outburst, Goo stands in the doorway of Foster's, eyes brimming with tears, quietly starting to leave while hundreds of her imaginary friends swarm the halls and Frankie teeters on the edge of collapse. But before she disappears out the front gates, Mac chases after her.

"Goo, wait!"

He apologizes — genuinely, not just because Bloo guilted him into it. He tells her she's not a freak. That her imagination is amazing. That he actually likes spending time with her, even when she talks a mile a minute about chupacabras and robot llama farms.

Goo's face lights up — and before Mac can react, she throws her arms around him in a massive hug.

And that's when it happens. Mac freezes. His heart does a little stutter-step. His face goes warm. *Oh no,* he thinks. *Oh no no no no.*

Goo pulls back, chattering happily: "See? Told ya you liked me!"

"I—I don't *like* like you!" Mac blurts, way too fast, way too defensive.

"Nobody said anything about *like*-like!" Goo grins.

They walk back into Foster's together, Mac staring at the floor the whole way and silently panicking, while Bloo watches from a window with the biggest smirk in recorded history. From then on, the deal stands — Goo only visits on Adopt-A-Thought Saturdays so the overcrowding stays controlled. Mac's crush, though, is a whole other problem, one he's determined to bury six feet under.

---

## How the Crush Thread Plays Through the Season

**"The Big Picture"** — During the annual house photo, Goo wedges herself right next to Mac, who stiffens like a board every time the photographer counts down. Bloo notices and spends the mystery subplot making kissing faces off-camera. When they solve the strange photo, Goo snaps the *real* photo herself — and in it, Mac is caught mid-glance at her, smiling. Bloo keeps a copy as blackmail material; Mac steals it back twice. It keeps reappearing.

**"Neighbor Pains"** — Goo's organizational genius saves Adopt-A-Thought Saturday, and Frankie declares her a legend. Mac, assigned as her "assistant," trips over his own words all day. When Goo says, "You're acting weird today," Mac answers, "I'm ALWAYS weird!" so loudly that Coco stops mid-cluck. Goo just shrugs, patient — she's known for a while. She's just waiting.

**"Infernal Slumber"** — Ultimate torture: Goo at Mac's *house*, in pajamas, three feet away, all night. He can't sleep — partly from keeping everyone quiet for his mom, partly because Goo keeps whispering "aren't slumber parties the BEST?" Every time she leans closer in the sleeping bag circle, Mac scoots back an inch until he's pressed against the wall. Eduardo, sweet and oblivious, offers to let Mac sleep on *his* tummy instead. Mac seriously considers it.

**"I Only Have Surprise for You"** — Mac is paranoid about the party, but *extra* paranoid about Goo, the world's worst secret-keeper. He spends half the episode dodging Bloo and the other half dodging Goo's very obvious "SO EXCITED FOR NOTHING IN PARTICULAR ON FRIDAY, AREN'T YOU?!" winks. When the party ambushes him anyway and Goo leaps out of the cake-shaped balloon, Mac — mid-scream — forgets to be annoyed for exactly one second.

**"Bus the Two of Us"** — Goo's crowning comedic moment: she conjures imaginary duplicates of Mac and Bloo to distract Frankie and Mr. Herriman. The fake Mac is perfect... except it keeps blushing and stammering whenever fake-Bloo teases it. Real Mac, watching from the bus, groans: "It doesn't do that!" Wilt and Bloo exchange a look. Goo just giggles: "It does a little."

**"The Big Cheese"** — Locked out of the mansion with Cheese the only one who knows the code, Goo is the one person whose chaotic mental frequency matches his. She extracts the code while Mac watches in open admiration — then catches himself and snaps his jaw shut. Bloo: "Saw that." Mac: "Saw NOTHING."

**"Make Believe It or Not"** — Goo's game-world villains imprison Mac and Bloo. While captive, Bloo — of all people — says, "You know she'd never actually hurt you, right? She invented a whole evil empire and *you're* still the main character in it." Mac, tied to a cardboard throne, finally goes quiet. When Goo defeats her own villains and frees them, Mac hugs her first. Goo, for once, is speechless. Then, after a beat: "...Finally."

**"Schlock Star"** — Goo as MC is electric: she hypes the crowd, invents a light show out of imaginary friends, and introduces Bloo's band with pure chaos energy. During the encore she grabs Mac's hand and yanks him onstage to dance. He protests the entire time — and does not let go of her hand once.

---

## "Goodbye to Bloo" — The Confession

The gang believes Mac is moving away forever and throws an elaborate farewell. Goo, who knew the truth the whole time (his mom had mentioned the promotion and the bigger apartment weeks ago during a Saturday visit), says nothing — because she's decided this is the moment.

She sings her nonsensical song — half gibberish, half something surprisingly tender — while Mac stands there baffled, because *he's not leaving the city, why is everyone crying?*

When the misunderstanding is revealed — just a move to a bigger apartment in the same complex for his mom's home office — everyone laughs with relief. But Mac walks straight up to Goo in front of *everybody*.

"You knew. This whole time. You knew I—"

"Knew what?" Goo teases, one eyebrow up.

Mac takes a breath. Eight years of being the only sane one at Foster's, and this is the bravest thing he's ever done.

"...I like-like you. I've liked-like you since the hug."

The mansion erupts. Bloo faints dramatically. Coco lays an egg out of pure shock. Wilt dabs his eye: "That was beautiful, man." Frankie insists she knew from day one; Mr. Herriman clears his throat about the "public spectacle"; Wilt grumbles about losing a bet to Bloo.

Goo just beams, spins in a circle, and creates seventeen imaginary friends on the spot just to high-five each other. Then she hugs Mac again — the same hug from that first rainy day — and this time, Mac doesn't freeze.

He hugs back.

"That's what I've been waiting for, silly," she whispers. "Took you long enough."

---

**Epilogue:** The bigger apartment means Mac's mom gets her home office — and the new place is even closer to Foster's, so Mac can visit more often. Goo's imaginary friends now only appear when invited. And every Adopt-A-Thought Saturday, two kids walk through the front gates hand in hand, while Bloo loudly demands royalties for "being the world's greatest matchmaker."

*The end.*

# The Internet of Things: A Comprehensive Report and Proposed Smart Campus Solution

## 1. Overview of the Internet of Things (IoT)

### 1.1 What is the Internet of Things?

The Internet of Things (IoT) refers to a network of interconnected physical devices—commonly called "smart" or "connected" devices—that are embedded with sensors, software, and other technologies enabling them to collect, exchange, and act upon data over the internet, often without direct human intervention. The term was coined by Kevin Ashton in 1999, and since then, IoT has grown from a conceptual idea into one of the most transformative technologies of the 21st century.

Unlike traditional internet usage, where humans create and consume data (e.g., browsing websites or sending emails), in IoT, *things*—such as sensors, appliances, vehicles, and wearable devices—generate and communicate data autonomously. Industry estimates suggest there are already well over 15 billion connected devices worldwide, a number expected to approach 30 billion by 2030.

### 1.2 How Does IoT Work?

IoT systems typically operate through four functional layers:

1. **Perception/Sensing Layer:** Physical devices equipped with sensors (temperature, motion, humidity, GPS, cameras, etc.) collect raw data from the environment.
2. **Network/Connectivity Layer:** Data is transmitted via communication technologies such as Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Zigbee, LoRaWAN, cellular networks (4G/5G), or NFC to a central processing point.
3. **Data Processing Layer:** Cloud platforms or edge computing devices process, store, and analyze the collected data, often using analytics or artificial intelligence.
4. **Application/User Layer:** End users interact with the system through dashboards, mobile applications, or automated alerts, while actuators may trigger physical actions (e.g., turning on a sprinkler).

```
 │   Mobile App │ Web Dashboard │ Alerts │ Reports         │

                             │

                             │

```

*Figure 1: The four-layer architecture of an IoT system, showing how data flows from physical sensors, through network communication, to cloud processing, and finally to end-user applications.*

A simple example: a smart thermostat senses room temperature (perception), sends the reading via Wi-Fi to a cloud server (network), the cloud compares it with user preferences (processing), and commands the thermostat to adjust cooling (application/actuation).

### 1.3 Advantages of IoT

- **Automation and Efficiency:** Devices operate autonomously, reducing manual labor and human error.
- **Real-Time Monitoring:** Instant access to data enables rapid decision-making (e.g., health monitoring, traffic management).
- **Cost Reduction:** Optimized resource usage—smart lighting and HVAC systems can cut energy bills by 20–30%.
- **Improved Quality of Life:** Smart homes, wearable health devices, and connected cars enhance comfort and safety.
- **Data-Driven Insights:** Continuous data collection enables predictive maintenance and better planning.

### 1.4 Disadvantages and Challenges of IoT

- **Security Vulnerabilities:** Connected devices are attractive targets for hackers; weak authentication and unpatched firmware are common entry points.
- **Privacy Concerns:** Devices continuously collect personal data, raising questions about surveillance and data ownership.
- **High Initial Cost:** Deploying sensors, networks, and platforms requires significant investment.
- **Interoperability Issues:** Devices from different manufacturers often use incompatible protocols and standards.
- **Dependence on Connectivity:** Internet outages or power failures can disable critical systems.
- **Data Overload:** Massive volumes of generated data require robust storage and processing infrastructure.

### 1.5 The Future of IoT

The future of IoT is closely tied to several emerging technologies:

- **5G Networks:** Ultra-low latency and high bandwidth will enable real-time applications such as autonomous vehicles and remote surgery.
- **Artificial Intelligence (AIoT):** Integrating AI with IoT will allow devices to make intelligent, predictive decisions rather than merely reporting data.
- **Edge Computing:** Processing data locally on devices will reduce latency, bandwidth costs, and privacy risks.
- **Digital Twins:** Virtual replicas of physical assets will enable simulation and optimization in industry and urban planning.
- **Smart Cities:** IoT will drive innovations in traffic management, waste collection, energy grids, and public safety.

As costs continue to fall and standards mature, IoT is expected to become as ubiquitous as electricity—largely invisible but fundamentally supporting daily life.

---

## 2. Problem Statement

University campuses and large office buildings consume enormous amounts of energy and resources, yet most are managed manually and inefficiently:

- **Energy Waste:** Lights and air conditioning are frequently left running in empty classrooms and offices, leading to inflated electricity bills and unnecessary carbon emissions.
- **Poor Space Utilization:** Students often waste time searching for available study rooms, and administrators lack data on how spaces are actually used.
- **Reactive Maintenance:** Equipment failures (e.g., broken projectors, water leaks, HVAC malfunctions) are discovered only after being reported by users, causing disruption and higher repair costs.
- **No Centralized Visibility:** Facility managers have no unified, real-time view of campus conditions, making informed decision-making impossible.

There is a clear need for an affordable, centralized IoT-based system that monitors and manages campus facilities in real time, reduces waste, and improves the experience of students and staff.

---

## 3. Existing Solutions

Several solutions currently exist, though each has limitations:

| Solution | Description | Limitations |
|---|---|---|
| **Commercial Building Management Systems (BMS)** | e.g., Honeywell, Siemens, Johnson Controls | Very expensive and complex; designed for large enterprises; unaffordable for smaller institutions |
| **Standalone Smart Devices** | Smart plugs, smart bulbs (e.g., Philips Hue, TP-Link) | Operate in silos; no unified campus-wide monitoring or analytics |
| **Booking Applications** | Room reservation apps | Rely on manual input; no automatic detection of actual occupancy |
| **Academic/Research Prototypes** | Various university IoT testbeds | Rarely integrated, scalable, or user-friendly for real deployment |

None of the existing solutions combine low cost, centralized real-time monitoring, automated control, and predictive maintenance in a single platform tailored for a campus environment. This gap motivates our proposed project.

---

## 4. Proposed Solution: Smart Campus IoT Platform (SCIP)

We propose the **Smart Campus IoT Platform (SCIP)**—an integrated, affordable system that uses IoT sensors and a centralized cloud dashboard to:

1. **Automatically control lighting and air conditioning** based on real-time occupancy detection, eliminating energy waste in empty rooms.
2. **Monitor classroom occupancy and availability**, displaying live room status on a mobile app so students can find free study spaces instantly.
3. **Detect environmental anomalies** (high temperature, water leaks, poor air quality) and trigger instant alerts for maintenance staff.
4. **Provide analytics dashboards** for administrators, showing energy consumption trends, room utilization rates, and maintenance predictions.
5. **Enable predictive maintenance** by analyzing equipment sensor data to forecast failures before they occur.

The system is designed using low-cost, off-the-shelf components and open-source software, making it deployable and scalable across an entire campus at a fraction of the cost of commercial BMS solutions.

---

## 5. Key Components of the Idea

| Component | Description |
|---|---|
| **ESP32 Microcontroller Nodes** | Low-cost Wi-Fi enabled boards deployed in each room, reading sensors and controlling actuators |
| **Sensors** | PIR motion sensors (occupancy), DHT22 (temperature/humidity), MQ-135 (air quality), current sensors (energy monitoring), water leak detectors |
| **Actuators** | Smart relays to switch lights and HVAC units on/off automatically |
| **Communication** | MQTT protocol over Wi-Fi for lightweight, reliable message exchange between devices and server |
| **Backend Server & MQTT Broker** | A central server (e.g., Node-RED or a Python backend) that receives sensor data, applies control rules, and stores data |
| **Cloud Database** | Time-series database (e.g., InfluxDB) storing historical sensor readings for analytics |
| **Web Dashboard** | Administrator interface showing real-time statuses, charts, alerts, and reports |
| **Mobile Application** | Student-facing app showing available rooms, campus notifications, and issue reporting |
| **Alerts Module** | Email/SMS/push notifications sent to maintenance staff upon anomaly detection |

# Chapter One: General Introduction

## 1.1 Background of the Study

The pursuit of sustained economic growth, macroeconomic stability, and poverty reduction remains the central objective of developing economies. Within the macroeconomic policy toolkit, fiscal policy—encompassing government expenditure, taxation, and public debt management—and monetary policy—conducted through interest rates, money supply, and exchange rate mechanisms—represent the two primary levers for influencing aggregate demand, stabilizing prices, and steering long-term development. The interaction between these two policy domains, whether complementary or contradictory, has profound implications for macroeconomic outcomes. While Keynesian traditions emphasize the potency of countercyclical fiscal policy, monetarist and rational expectations perspectives accord primacy to monetary discipline or warn against the crowding-out effects of deficit financing (Friedman, 1968; Barro, 1974; Sargent & Wallace, 1981). Contemporary consensus, however, stresses the *policy mix*—the strategic coordination of fiscal and monetary instruments—arguing that the effectiveness of one is inherently contingent upon the design and posture of the other.

In Sub-Saharan Africa, this coordination carries particular significance. Many countries have historically experienced fiscal dominance, whereby persistent budget deficits force monetary authorities to accommodate government financing needs at the expense of price stability. The Structural Adjustment Programs (SAPs) of the 1980s and 1990s, followed by the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) debt relief initiatives of the early 2000s, reshaped the continent's policy landscape, imposing greater fiscal discipline and fostering more autonomous central banks.

Cameroon presents a compelling case study within this context. As the largest economy in the Central African Economic and Monetary Community (CEMAC), it operates within a distinctive institutional dichotomy: monetary policy is centralized at the supranational level under the Bank of Central African States (BEAC), while fiscal policy remains under national sovereignty. The fixed peg of the CFA franc—first to the French franc and, since 1999, to the euro—supported by the French Treasury's convertibility guarantee through the Operations Account, constrains national monetary autonomy and elevates the relative importance of fiscal instruments. Under the Mundell–Fleming "impossible trinity," this configuration means that the burden of macroeconomic stabilization and development financing falls disproportionately on national fiscal policy, yet Cameroon's fiscal landscape is marked by low non-oil revenue mobilization, rising public debt, and procyclical spending linked to volatile commodity prices.

Over the past three decades, Cameroon has navigated a series of defining economic episodes: the severe crisis of the late 1980s and early 1990s, culminating in the 50% devaluation of the CFA franc in January 1994 alongside IMF-supported adjustment programs; debt relief under the HIPC and Multilateral Debt Relief Initiatives in the mid-2000s; the ambitious Vision 2035 framework and its operational strategies (the Document de Stratégie pour la Croissance et l'Emploi, DSCE, and the Stratégie Nationale de Développement 2020–2030, SND30); and, more recently, severe shocks including the 2014 oil price collapse, the Boko Haram insurgency in the Far North, the Anglophone socio-political crisis, the COVID-19 pandemic, and the global inflationary pressures of 2022–2023. Throughout these episodes, Cameroonian authorities have deployed a mix of fiscal measures—public investment programs, tax reforms, budget consolidation—and monetary-cum-financial measures orchestrated within the CEMAC framework, including BEAC policy rates, reserve requirements, and banking sector reforms. The extent to which this combined policy mix has contributed to—or failed to deliver—meaningful economic development remains an open empirical question, motivating the present study.

## 1.2 Statement of the Problem

Despite a substantial theoretical and empirical literature on fiscal–monetary interactions, the evidence remains inconclusive, particularly for developing economies operating within monetary unions. Existing studies on Cameroon and CEMAC more broadly have produced mixed findings: some attribute periods of growth acceleration to expansionary fiscal stances, others highlight the inflationary consequences of monetary accommodation, and still others point to weak coordination between the Ministry of Finance and BEAC as a persistent source of macroeconomic instability.

Several gaps warrant attention. First, much of the empirical work examines fiscal and monetary policies in isolation, neglecting interaction effects and the possibility that the combined policy mix produces outcomes distinct from the sum of individual policies. Second, few studies adopt a longitudinal perspective spanning the major structural breaks of the past three decades—the 1994 devaluation, the HIPC process, and the recent pandemic shock—which are essential for understanding how the effectiveness of the policy mix has evolved. Third, the literature often focuses narrowly on GDP growth, whereas economic development encompasses broader dimensions, including price stability, investment, employment, debt sustainability, and structural transformation. Fourth, the role of Cameroon's specific institutional setting—membership in a monetary union with a fixed exchange rate and oil dependency—remains underexplored as a conditioning factor for policy effectiveness. This study addresses these gaps by systematically exploring the existing literature and analyzing how the combined fiscal and monetary policy stance has shaped Cameroon's economic development over the past three decades (approximately 1994–2024).

## 1.3 Research Questions

The central question guiding this research is: **How have combined fiscal and monetary policies shaped Cameroon's economic development over the past three decades?**

This is decomposed into the following specific questions:

1. What does the existing theoretical and empirical literature reveal about the individual and combined effects of fiscal and monetary policies on economic development in developing and Sub-Saharan African economies?
2. What have been the major fiscal and monetary policy orientations adopted in Cameroon (and at the CEMAC level) between 1994 and 2024, and how have they evolved across key economic episodes?
3. What are the relative and interactive effects of fiscal and monetary policy instruments on Cameroon's growth and broader development indicators, and does "fiscal dominance" or "monetary dominance" better characterize the country's macroeconomic framework?
4. What lessons can be drawn for improving fiscal–monetary coordination in Cameroon and comparable CEMAC economies?

## 1.4 Objectives of the Study

**Main objective:** To review the existing literature and analyze how combined fiscal and monetary policies have shaped Cameroon's economic development over the past three decades (1994–2024).

**Specific objectives:**

1. To critically explore and synthesize the theoretical and empirical literature on the effects of fiscal policy, monetary policy, and their interaction on economic development, with emphasis on monetary unions.
2. To trace the evolution of fiscal and monetary policy regimes in Cameroon, situating them within the institutional context of the CEMAC union and the fixed exchange rate regime.
3. To empirically estimate the individual and combined (interactive) effects of fiscal and monetary policy instruments on Cameroon's development outcomes, using appropriate econometric techniques.
4. To formulate evidence-based recommendations for enhanced macroeconomic policy coordination in support of Cameroon's structural transformation and SND30 goals.

## 1.5 Significance of the Study

**Theoretically and academically**, the study contributes to the sparse literature on macroeconomic policy coordination in the CEMAC region, enriching the debate on the limits of sovereign fiscal policy in the absence of national monetary autonomy. **Empirically**, it provides a cohesive, long-term retrospective analysis bridging historical qualitative documentation and quantitative econometric studies, adopting an interaction-focused framework across major structural breaks. **Methodologically**, it combines a systematic literature review with econometric analysis in a manner replicable for other monetary union members. **Practically**, the findings are of direct utility to Cameroonian policymakers (Ministry of Finance; Ministry of Economy, Planning and Regional Development), BEAC, development partners (IMF, World Bank, African Development Bank), and civil society, by identifying which policy configurations have been most conducive to development outcomes.

## 1.6 Scope and Limitations

**Conceptual scope:** Fiscal policy is operationalized through government expenditure, tax revenue, and budget balance; monetary policy through money supply (M2), policy/interest rates, and inflation. Economic development is proxied primarily by real GDP growth, with supplementary attention to inflation, investment, public debt, and per capita income. **Geographical scope:** Cameroon, framed within the CEMAC institutional architecture. **Temporal scope:** approximately 1994–2024, capturing the post-devaluation adjustment, the HIPC era, the 2014 oil shock, and the recent poly-crisis. **Data sources:** World Bank World Development Indicators, IMF statistics and country reports, BEAC publications, and Cameroon's National Institute of Statistics (INS).

**Limitations:** Macroeconomic time series in developing countries frequently undergo structural breaks, base-year revisions, and inconsistencies across national and international databases. Moreover, because BEAC's monetary policy decisions apply to the entire CEMAC zone rather than Cameroon alone, disentangling the precise national impact of supranational decisions presents methodological complexity.

## 1.7 Organization of the Thesis

The thesis is structured into five chapters. **Chapter One** presents this introduction. **Chapter Two** reviews the theoretical and empirical literature on fiscal policy, monetary policy, and their combined effects, culminating in the identification of gaps and a conceptual framework. **Chapter Three** establishes the institutional and macroeconomic context of Cameroon from 1994 to 2024 and details the methodology, data, and estimation techniques. **Chapter Four** presents and discusses the empirical results. **Chapter Five** concludes with policy recommendations, limitations, and directions for future research.

# Presentation Guide: Singapore English (Singlish) — Orthoepy in Global Context

Below is a well-researched, ready-to-adapt guide with content for your slides, a suggested structure, and delivery tips for a video presentation.

## 1. Framing: What Is Singapore English?

Singapore English exists on a **continuum** (classic diglossia, per Anthea Fraser Gupta's model):

- **Standard Singapore English (SSE)** — the acrolect: used in government, education, news, and international business; grammatically close to Standard British/American English but with a distinctly local accent.
- **Colloquial Singapore English (Singlish/CSE)** — the basilect: a creole-influenced contact variety shaped by **Hokkien, Cantonese, Teochew, Mandarin, Malay, and Tamil**.

Key framing point: Singlish is **not "broken English"** — it is a systematic, rule-governed variety, a point linguists (Gupta, Lisa Lim, David Deterding, Jakob Leimgruber) have established firmly. It also fits Braj Kachru's **Outer Circle** in the World Englishes paradigm.

---

## 2. Pronunciation & Orthoepy (Your Core Section — Demonstrate Aloud!)

**Consonants**
- **Th-stopping:** /θ/, /ð/ → [t], [d]: *three* → "tree," *this* → "dis" (Malay, Hokkien, and Tamil lack dental fricatives).
- **Final consonant cluster reduction / unreleased stops:** *act* → [ɛk̚], *text* → "tex"; final stops often glottalized.
- **Final devoicing:** *of* → "off," *live* → "lif".
- **L-vocalization:** *milk* → "miuk," *cool* → "coo".
- **Non-rhoticity:** *car* → "cah".

**Vowels**
- **Monophthongization of diphthongs:** *face* → [feːs], *go* → [goː].
- **Mergers of tense/lax pairs:** *seat/sit*, *pool/pull* sound alike; also *bad/bed* for some speakers.
- **Less vowel reduction:** full vowels where RP would use schwa — this contributes to the "staccato" sound.

**Prosody (the most distinctive feature)**
- **Syllable-timed rhythm** (vs. stress-timed British/American English) — every syllable gets roughly equal weight, giving the "machine-gun" pace.
- **Distinctive stress placement:** *character* → "cha-RAK-ter," *hotel* → "HO-tel".
- **Particles carry tone**, echoing Sinitic tonal systems; rising final contours on statements are markers of solidarity, not questions.

> Orthoepy insight: these are **systematic, predictable patterns**, not errors — exactly what a descriptive study of pronunciation should document. Cite Deterding's acoustic work.

---

## 3. Grammar (Substrate Transfer from Chinese & Malay)

1. **Copula deletion:** "This place damn hot." / "She my sister."
2. **Topic-prominence:** "This book, I read already."
3. **No tense inflection; adverbs + aspect markers:** "Yesterday he go work"; "**already**" as perfective ("I eat already"); "**ever**" as experiential ("You ever go Japan?").
4. **"Got" as existential/possessive:** "Got people here"; "I got see him."
5. **A-not-A questions:** "You want eat or not?"; **"Can or not?"**; invariant tag **"Is it?"** ("You're coming, is it?").
6. **"Can" as a full response:** "Can!" (= yes, possible); "Cannot lah."
7. **"One" as emphatic/nominalizer** (from Chinese 的): "He so stubborn one."
8. **"Kena"** (Malay) as passive marker: "He kena scolded."
9. **Reduplication:** "walk-walk" (casual strolling), "small-small boy," "wait long long."
10. **No plural -s with numerals/quantifiers:** "three book."

---

## 4. Vocabulary & Expressions

**Borrowings:** *kiasu* (Hokkien, "fear of losing out" — in the OED), *kiasi* ("afraid to die"), *shiok* (fantastic), *makan* (eat, Malay), *kena* (Malay), *paiseh* (embarrassed), *sian* (bored), *jialat* (in deep trouble), *chim/cheem* (profound), *sabo* (sabotage/prank), *chope* (reserve a seat — famously with a tissue packet), *ang moh* (Westerner), *atas* (posh, Malay), *sotong* (squid; "blur like sotong" = clueless), *lepak* (loiter), *alamak* (oh no), *tapao* (takeaway), *aiyoh/aiyah* (exclamations).

**Localized English words:** *blur* (clueless), *stay* (reside: "I stay in Jurong"), *send* (accompany/take: "I send you home"), *open/off* (turn on/off the light/fan), *follow* (understand).

**Discourse particles — the signature of Singlish:**
| Particle | Function |
|---|---|
| **lah** | emphasis, solidarity, reassurance ("Don't worry lah") |
| **leh** | mild contradiction/softening ("Not bad leh") |
| **lor** | resignation, stating the obvious ("Like that lor") |
| **meh** | skepticism ("Really meh?") |
| **liao** | completion ("I eat liao") |
| **hor** | seeking agreement ("Nice hor?") |
| **sia** | emphasis/exclamation ("Shiok sia!") |

**Idioms:** "Can lah!" / "Can or not?" / "Where got?" (= no way!), "Don't play play" (don't mess around), "So how?" (what now?), "Confirm plus chop" (absolutely certain), "Die die must try," "Catch no ball" (from Hokkien *liak bo kiu* — don't understand at all), "Steady lah!"

## 5. Sociolinguistics & Global Impact

1. **History:** English arrived via British colonization (Raffles, 1819), served as the interethnic lingua franca, and became an official language and school medium after independence (1965). Singlish grew as a contact creole.
2. **The Speak Good English Movement (2000–):** Government campaign against Singlish, citing economic competitiveness and international intelligibility — a globally cited **language-policy case study** in the standardization vs. identity debate.
3. **Identity:** Singlish thrives as a pan-ethnic badge of Singaporean identity — the one variety all groups share (media examples: *Phua Chu Kang*, *I Not Stupid*, local comedy and social media).
4. **Lexical export:** *kiasu*, *shiok*, *lah* appear in major dictionaries; Singlish circulates globally via media (e.g., *Crazy Rich Asians*, Singaporean YouTubers/creators) and diaspora communities.
5. **Intelligibility research (Deterding & Kirkpatrick):** SSE is highly intelligible internationally; heavy basilectal Singlish is less so to outsiders — showing that intelligibility is **graded and context-dependent**.
6. **Code-switching dexterity:** Singaporeans pivot between SSE and Singlish by domain — a live model of **English as a Lingua Franca** competence: accommodation, not monocentric norms.
7. **Big-picture lesson:** English is **pluricentric**; an Outer-Circle variety can serve law, trade, and technology with its own phonology and pragmatics. Orthoepy must therefore be **descriptive, not prescriptive**.

# Deceased Estates & Maintenance under ASX Requirements — An Introductory Guide

This is general educational information, not legal or compliance advice. The governing framework is the **ASX Settlement Operating Rules**, the *Corporations Act 2001* (notably Part 6.7, covering transmission applications), and each broker (ASX "Participant") and share registry's own procedures. Always confirm against the current rulebook and your organisation's procedures.

## Background

- **CHESS** (Clearing House Electronic Subregister System) holds uncertificated holdings against a **HIN** (Holder Identification Number), sponsored by a Participant (broker). Issuer-sponsored holdings are managed by the share registry instead.
- When a holder dies, their holdings must be dealt with through survivorship or the estate before they can be transferred, sold, or retained. Locks and suspensions exist to protect the estate, beneficiaries, and the Participant from unauthorised dealings in the meantime.

---

## a) Survivorship Requests

**What it is:** Where securities are held as **joint tenants** (e.g., a couple jointly), the deceased's interest passes automatically to the surviving holder(s) under the right of survivorship — it does **not** form part of the estate.

**Process / requirements:**
- The surviving holder (or their Participant) lodges a **Request to Register by Survivorship** (or registry-equivalent form) with a **certified death certificate** and verification of identity.
- A **Grant of Probate is not required** for a true joint-tenancy holding — the surviving joint proprietor is entitled regardless of what the Will says about executors.
- The registry removes the deceased and re-registers the survivor as sole holder; on the CHESS side this is typically effected by amending registration details or establishing a new HIN for the survivor and transferring the stock off the joint HIN, after which the joint HIN may be closed.

**Watch-outs:**
- **Tenants in common do not get survivorship** — the deceased's share falls into the estate and is handled via transmission/probate.
- Check whether the holding is CHESS-sponsored (Participant handles) or issuer-sponsored (registry handles).

## b) Deceased and Non-Deceased Estate HIN Locks and Unlocks

**Deceased estate locks:**
- On notification of death, the Participant applies a lock to the HIN (via internal back-office controls and/or CHESS maintenance messages) to **freeze trading and transfers** pending verification of estate documents. Any open market orders must be purged.
- The lock protects the estate from unauthorised or accidental dealings and prevents disputes between beneficiaries.

**Unlocks:**
- The lock is released only when authority is verified — typically a certified **Grant of Probate or Letters of Administration** plus instructions from the executor/administrator (the Legal Personal Representative).
- Note: often the HIN is not simply unlocked for normal trading; it may be unlocked temporarily solely to allow an off-market transfer to the executor's estate HIN or to beneficiaries, after which the original HIN is closed.

**Non-deceased estate locks:**
- HINs may also be locked for other reasons: disputes, suspected fraud, court orders, bankruptcy, failed settlement, or regulatory/AML flags (e.g., sanctions). Unlocks require documented justification and appropriate authorisation (court order, clearance of the underlying issue, compliance sign-off).
- Locks are a **risk-control overlay** — they restrict dealings but do not change legal ownership.

## c) HIN Cancellation Requests

A HIN can only be cancelled once the account is genuinely empty:

**Pre-requisites:**
1. **Zero balance** — all securities transferred out (off-market transfer, conversion to issuer sponsorship, or sold and settled).
2. **No pending activity** — no outstanding settlements, unsettled corporate actions or dividends, or active orders.
3. **No active locks** — locks must be removed before cancellation is processed.

**Deceased estate context:**
- After transmission to the executor/beneficiaries or liquidation of holdings, cancelling the deceased's HIN is the final administrative step. The Participant lodges the CHESS cancellation/maintenance instruction (MT537/MT538-type holder maintenance messages), supported by the estate documentation.

**Other contexts:** Cancellation also applies to ordinary account closures, holder consolidation, or moving to another Participant, with proper client instruction and records.

## d) Deceased International Account Suspensions

International holdings (e.g., US, UK) are usually held via an **omnibus/custody arrangement** with a foreign custodian, not on CHESS — so the account is **suspended** rather than HIN-locked.

- **Immediate suspension** on notification of death, to prevent trading and preserve foreign tax/regulatory compliance.
- **Documentation:** certified death certificate, foreign grant of probate or resealing of the Australian grant where the foreign jurisdiction requires it (e.g., UK and some Commonwealth jurisdictions recognise reseals), translations, and executor ID verification.
- **US "situs" assets:** if a non-US resident held US shares valued over roughly **USD 60,000** at date of death, US federal estate tax rules apply; the custodian may require an **IRS Transfer Certificate** (Form 706-NA process) before releasing assets.
- **Release:** the suspension is lifted once the custodian's compliance clears the tax and probate requirements, after which assets can be transferred or repatriated. Foreign processes are typically slower and stricter than domestic ones.

---

## Practical Checklist

1. Identify holding type: joint tenancy vs tenants in common; CHESS vs issuer-sponsored; domestic vs international.
2. Confirm death with a certified certificate; note the date of death.
3. Apply the right control: survivorship request, estate HIN lock, or international suspension.
4. Obtain authority documents: probate/letters of administration, survivorship form, foreign grant/reseal as needed.
5. Lodge the transmission/transfer instruction with full audit trail.
6. Reconcile dividends and corporate action entitlements before closing.
7. Cancel the HIN once zero balance and no pending activity.
8. Document the basis for every lock, unlock, cancellation and suspension.

## Tips

- **Probate thresholds vary by registry and company** — many will transmit small holdings without a grant, which can save significant time and cost.
- Contact each **share registry** (Computershare, Link Group, MUFG) early — forms and evidence requirements differ.
- Work closely with the Participant's deceased estates/maintenance team, who apply the locks, unlocks, and cancellations.

# Incorporating Higher-Than-Expected Claims Inflation in Reserves

## Why standard methods are challenged

Standard techniques (e.g. the basic chain ladder) implicitly assume that the inflation environment embedded in historical development patterns will continue into the future. When inflation rises above that embedded level, projections based on past experience will understate future claim payments. The actuary therefore needs methods that either correct for the historical inflation implicit in the data or explicitly assume higher future inflation.

## Methods

### 1. Inflation indexation / "deflate–reflate" approach
- Adjust historical claims triangles to constant price levels using an appropriate index (CPI, medical cost index, wage index, claims-specific index), removing the lower historical inflation.
- Apply a standard reserving method (chain ladder, BF, etc.) to the deflated data.
- Reflate projected future payments using an **explicit higher future inflation assumption**, possibly ramped (elevated for a period, then reverting to a long-run level).

### 2. Explicit assumption adjustment within existing models
- Replace the inflation assumption in the current reserving model with a higher one (point uplift or phased path) and re-run the projection.
- Targeted to lines most exposed (e.g. bodily injury, motor repair, property).

### 3. Calendar-year / separation methods
- Inflation is a **calendar-year effect** (affects all claims settled in a period regardless of origin). Methods that separate accident year, development and calendar-year parameters (e.g. Taylor/Verbeek separation, GLMs with calendar-year parameters, Munich chain ladder variants) allow the actuary to overwrite future calendar-year parameters with the new inflation forecast.

### 4. Frequency–severity modelling
- Model claim counts and average costs separately; inflation applies mainly to **severity** (with appropriate settlement lag). Different inflation assumptions can be applied by cost driver (repair costs, medical, wages, court awards), and frequency adjusted if economic conditions change claim propensity.

### 5. Adjustment to standard triangle selections
- Adjust development factor selections to reflect recent higher inflation (e.g. re-weight recent periods), or increase tail factors.
- Increase the a priori expected loss ratios in **Bornhuetter–Ferguson / Cape Cod** methods to reflect the higher inflation outlook; BF-type methods are relatively insensitive to distorted recent experience, so the adjustment can be applied cleanly to the prior.

### 6. Judgmental overlay / reserve loading
- Apply a documented post-model loading to the aggregate reserve, calibrated from sensitivity analysis or market intelligence. Transparent and easy to communicate, but risks being arbitrary unless supported by analysis; must be governed and reconciled.

### 7. Case reserve / individual claim review
- Re-estimate large or long-tail outstanding case reserves at current cost levels (updated repair estimates, medical projections). Care is needed to avoid double-counting if claims handlers have already increased case reserves for inflation.

### 8. Stochastic modelling and scenario/stress testing
- Treat inflation as a stochastic variable within a bootstrap, GLM or Bayesian framework, producing a reserve distribution reflecting inflation uncertainty.
- Run deterministic sensitivities/stresses (e.g. inflation +1%, +3%, +5% above base; persistent vs. transient) to quantify reserve sensitivity, inform risk margins/ASR, and communicate ranges.

### 9. External indices and benchmarking
- Use claims-specific external indices (construction costs, medical inflation, litigation trends) rather than generic CPI where the mismatch matters; benchmark against industry data.

## Factors in choosing a method

**1. Tail length / speed of settlement.** Short-tail classes: inflation passes through quickly and recent experience already reflects it, so simple adjustments may suffice. Long-tail classes: compounding over many years of settlement makes explicit indexation or calendar-year methods necessary.

**2. Nature and expected duration of the inflation.** Is the surge transient (supply shock) or persistent (wage-price spiral)? Drives a phased vs. permanent uplift.

**3. Type of inflation exposure.** Headline CPI vs. component-specific drivers (spare parts, building materials, medical costs, wage inflation) vs. social inflation (litigation costs). Some exposures are capped (policy limits); reinsurance structures may limit or transmit inflation effects.

**4. Data availability and credibility.** Sufficient, consistent history to identify inflation effects separately from development? Availability of reliable matching indices? Sparse or distorted data may force simpler, judgmental approaches.

**5. Materiality and proportionality.** If inflation-sensitive reserves are small, a simple loading may be adequate; material exposure justifies more sophisticated modelling. Cost/time/expertise should be proportionate.

**6. Distortions in recent experience.** Recent data may be contaminated (supply shocks, changed claim behaviour, altered case-reserving strength); the actuary must judge whether recent experience is predictive or distorted, and whether incurred data already reflect inflation (risk of double-counting).

**7. Degree of uncertainty in the outlook.** High uncertainty supports sensitivity/scenario ranges and possibly a prudent margin rather than a single point assumption.

**8. Interaction with other assumptions.** Consistency with discount rates (higher inflation may coincide with higher yields if reserving on a discounted basis), expense inflation, reinsurance recoveries, pricing, capital modelling and business plans.

**9. Regulatory, accounting and professional requirements.** Framework (IFRS 17 risk adjustment, Solvency II best estimate + risk margin, US GAAP) dictates whether a best-estimate or prudent basis applies and how margins are recognised; assumptions must be documented, justifiable and reviewable. Transparent methods (explicit assumptions, overlays) are easier to audit than subtle changes to factor selections.

**10. Communication.** Management, auditors and regulators must understand the assumption and its uncertainty; scenario analysis may communicate risk better than a single adjusted number.

## Conclusion

No single method is best in all circumstances. In practice the actuary will typically combine approaches: deflate and reflate historical data using claims-specific indices, apply explicit (possibly phased) future inflation assumptions, use BF/Cape Cod priors where recent experience is distorted, run sensitivities and stresses, and apply a documented overlay where justified — with the choice proportionate to materiality, tail characteristics, data quality and the need for transparent, defensible, internally consistent assumptions.

# Part One: The 7:42 to Northwood

The morning the world ended, Elias Vance was thinking about a broken radio.

He sat in his usual window seat on the 7:42 commuter train, third car from the front, with a disassembled transistor receiver spread across his knees like a patient on an operating table. At seventeen, Elias was tall and thin, with dark hair that fell into his eyes and fingers permanently stained with flux. While other kids collected sneakers or game consoles, Elias collected components — resistors, salvaged speakers, wire spools — all tucked into the olive-green canvas bag that clanked faintly when he walked. Today he was trying to figure out why the radio's audio stage had died, and the answer, he suspected, was a cracked solder joint he couldn't quite see.

The train rattled through the grey October morning toward the city, past strip malls and storage yards, carrying its usual half-asleep cargo. Across the aisle, an elderly woman named Mrs. Hollis — a retired music teacher who rode this train every day and always smelled of peppermints — was doing the crossword. Behind him, two businessmen argued in low voices about quarterly numbers. A cluster of students from St. Brendan's, in their maroon blazers, laughed too loudly over a phone screen.

"Your mother works nights again?" Mrs. Hollis asked, peering over her crossword. She'd adopted Elias months ago, in the way lonely commuters adopt each other.

"Three nights this week," Elias said. "She's a nurse at St. Cuthbert's. They're short-staffed. She said something about people coming in with... bites." He frowned. "Weird dog attacks, she thought."

"Bites?" Mrs. Hollis lowered her pen. "That's the second time I've heard that this week. My neighbour, Doris, said her grandson was bitten at a bus stop downtown and the wound went bad terribly fast. They wouldn't let her visit him at the hospital." She shook her head. "Whatever happened to a bit of flu and a doctor's note?"

Elias shrugged and bent back over the radio. The train hummed. The world was ordinary.

Then the brakes screamed.

It was not the gentle sigh of a normal stop. It was a full-emergency, metal-on-metal shriek that hurled everyone forward at once. Elias's radio flew from his lap and shattered against the seat ahead. Laptops crashed to the floor. A woman screamed. The train bucked, shuddered, and ground to a halt with a final groan, the lights flickering twice before settling into a sickly half-glow.

Silence. Then the conductor's voice over the intercom, strained and wrong: *"Ladies and gentlemen... please remain seated. There has been... an incident on the track. Please remain seated. Emergency services have been called. Please."*

"An incident," repeated one of the businessmen hollowly. "Incident means a person. It means a person on the tracks."

Faces pressed to windows all down the carriage. Elias didn't want to look, but his body carried him into the aisle like everyone else. Ahead, near the front of the train, he could see them: the driver and conductor standing on the gravel beside the tracks, hats off, and a knot of passengers who had climbed down despite every instruction. And between the rails, a shape.

It was a man. Had been a man. He lay folded across the rails in a way no living body could bend, and a dark stain was spreading slowly across the gravel beneath him, steaming faintly in the cold air. One of the passengers — a heavyset man in a green coat — crouched near the body and then reeled backward, hands clamped over his mouth. Elias saw the conductor turn away and be sick against a signal post.

"Oh, God," Mrs. Hollis whispered beside him. "Oh, the poor soul. The poor family."

The intercom crackled. "The... the authorities are on their way. We'll be held at this location. I apologize. Everyone — I'm so sorry."

The carriage broke apart after that, the way crowds do when horror needs somewhere to go. Some people sat and stared at their knees. Some called loved ones with no signal to carry the calls. A girl from St. Brendan's wept quietly into her blazer sleeve.

Elias gathered the broken pieces of his radio, not because they mattered, but because his hands needed work. Mrs. Hollis patted his arm without a word.

They sat there for forty minutes. Then the crowd in front of the train began to thin — people climbing the embankment toward the road, walking toward the city in straggling groups, unwilling to spend their morning trapped beside a body. Elias looked at his watch: 8:15. Northwood High was a mile and a half away. He could walk it and still make first period.

"I'm going to walk," he told Mrs. Hollis. "Come with me. There's a café near the school — I'll buy you a coffee and you can wait for a replacement bus."

"That's very sweet, love." She hesitated, glancing down the aisle. "But my knees..."

"There's a shortcut over the footbridge. Flat the whole way. Please — I'd feel better."

She smiled, tucked her crossword into her handbag, and took his arm.

They climbed the embankment steps together and came out onto Ringwell Road, a long grey avenue lined with linden trees that ran straight toward the city's northern districts. It was quieter than it should have been at rush hour. A few cars passed. A delivery van idled outside the bakery with its hazard lights on and no driver. Elias noticed, and filed it away, and kept walking.

They were perhaps halfway to the school when the running started.

A man in a tracksuit came sprinting around the corner ahead of them, face white, breath sawing. He didn't slow, didn't look at them, just pounded past with a strangled "Run — *run* —" thrown over his shoulder. Behind him came a woman in a waitress's apron, then a teenage boy still carrying a skateboard, then more — a dozen, two dozen people pouring out of the side streets, all fleeing in the same direction, away from the city center.

"What on earth—" Mrs. Hollis began.

The sound reached them next. It was not screaming, not exactly. It was a chorus — a wet, clicking, chattering noise like a thousand teeth, threaded with high, thin moans. Elias's skin crawled. He had heard that sound before, he realized, in fragments — in his mother's clipped voice on the phone at 2 a.m., in the sirens he'd slept through. But never whole. Never approaching.

Then the corner filled with them.

They came around the bend in a loose, lurching flood, and the world Elias understood simply stopped. They looked like people — a postman, a businessman, a woman in a floral dress — but everything human had been drained from their faces. Their skin was grey-white, mottled like old fruit. Their eyes were clouded, milky, rolling in sockets that could not fix on anything. Their jaws hung open, and that chattering sound poured out of them — the sound of hunger, he understood at once, the sound of mouths that had forgotten every word.

They were tearing the running crowd apart.

Elias saw it happen thirty meters away and would carry it forever: a man in a grey suit stumbled at the curb, and three of the things came down on him like dogs, and his screaming lasted four seconds and then became a different, wetter sound. The waitress turned and swung her handbag at one of them; it caught her by the wrist and *bit*, and she went down under three more.

"Mrs. Hollis." Elias's voice came out surprisingly level — some cold compartment of his mind had already taken over, cataloguing, analyzing, the way it did with circuit diagrams. *They're not looking at us. They turned toward the scream, not the runner. Sight is nothing to them.* "Mrs. Hollis, take my hand. We're going to walk — not run — to the school. Quietly. Do not scream. Do not speak. Nod if you understand."

She nodded, tears sliding down her face, and gripped his hand with surprising strength.

They moved along the hedge line, slow and quiet, while the world behind them tore itself open. Twice, one of the things lurched near, head tilting, nostrils flaring — *smelling*, Elias realized with a lurch of horror, they hunt by smell — and both times he steered them upwind behind a parked van and they drifted past, blind and clicking, chasing nothing.

A car alarm went off two streets over. Every head in the horde snapped toward the sound at once, a single coordinated motion that was somehow worse than anything else he'd seen, and the flood changed direction, pouring toward the noise like water finding a drain. Elias used the opening. He half-carried Mrs. Hollis across the last intersection, through the gap in the school's chain-link fence by the back lot, and up to the fire door of the east wing — locked.

He pounded, then stopped himself, then knocked softly in a rhythm. A face appeared at the wire-glass panel: Mr. Dobbs, the caretaker, sixty years old and grey-faced with terror, a crowbar in his hands.

"Vance? That's — you're the electronics kid." He hauled the door open. "In, in, QUICKLY —"

Elias pushed Mrs. Hollis through and slipped in after, and Mr. Dobbs slammed the door and dropped a steel bar into its brackets.

The east wing corridor was dim and silent. A handful of people cowered against the walls: two teachers — Ms. Reyes from biology, a small woman with a clipboard she was gripping like a weapon — and Mr. Okafor, the young physics teacher, and maybe a dozen students.

"Ground floor's a death trap," Mr. Dobbs rasped. "The things got in through the bus loop twenty minutes ago. We got maybe thirty people up to the third floor before the stairwell got... busy."

"Third floor?" Elias said. "Science labs. Heavy fire doors, high windows." He was already moving. "We should be higher. And those fire doors self-latch — the magnetic locks fail *open* on fire alarm. We need to be sure no one pulls an alarm."

"Fourth floor's storage and the old attic rooms," Mr. Okafor said. "Solid doors. There's a service stair."

They went up in a quiet, huddled column, Elias carrying Mrs. Hollis's bag, everyone stepping on the edges of the treads where the concrete wouldn't boom. On the third-floor landing, a fire door was barricaded with desks, and from behind it came muffled sobbing and a hissed voice — *"Shut up, you'll bring them —"* — and Elias's chest tightened, but there was no time, and he made himself keep climbing.

The fourth floor was a long corridor of storage rooms and the old science annex. And here Elias did the thing that would define the rest of his life.

The first storage room was locked from inside. He knocked — softly, three times — and a frightened voice said, "Who is it?"

"Elias Vance. Student. There are more of us. We're clearing this floor. Open the door, we'll explain everything."

"They said not to open —"

"The things outside track sound and smell, not sight," Elias said. "People locked in alone, crying, are exactly what they'll find if this floor stays scattered. Together, on one floor, behind two barricaded stairwells — that's survivable. Please."

A long pause. Then the bolt slid back, and the door opened on a cluster of eleven people — students, a lunch lady named Mrs. Petrov still in her apron, an art teacher with a broken wrist already splinted with a ruler and tape. Elias went door to door down the corridor, and the floor came alive: twenty here, fifteen there, a group of terrified freshmen pulled from the old audio-visual storeroom where they'd hidden among projector screens. word spread, doors opened, faces emerged. By the time the work was done, the fourth floor held nearly a hundred souls.

Then came the barricades. Mr. Okafor organized it with a teacher's instinct for delegating: desks, filing cabinets, the steel shelving from the storage rooms, everything with weight went to the tops of the two stairwells. Elias, at Mr. Dobbs's mutter of *"you're the one with the tools, lad,"* wire-tightened the shelving units to the door frames with copper wire from his bag, cross-braced, and jammed a fire axe handle through the push-bar of the main stair door so it could not be depressed from below. It was ugly work. It was strong work.

When it was done, they gathered in the central corridor, a hundred people in a loose, exhausted ring, and that was when the leader appeared.

He had not introduced himself during the work. He was a tall, silver-templed man in a rumpled suit jacket — a substitute teacher, Elias learned later, Mr. Aldous Crane — and he climbed onto a desk in the middle of the corridor and simply waited, and the crowd hushed on its own.

"My name is Aldous Crane," he said, and his voice carried without being raised. "Some of you know me. Most of you don't. That doesn't matter. What matters is what I'm about to say, so listen.

"Outside, an hour ago, civilization stopped. I don't know the cause. I don't know the cure. I know only this: the dead are walking, they are killing everything that lives, and no one is coming to save us before nightfall. Perhaps not after it.

"Now. I've watched you for the last hour. I saw Mr. Okafor organize the barricades. I saw Mr. Dobbs hold a door with a crowbar while children got past him. I saw a seventeen-year-old talk frightened strangers out of locked rooms and then wire those rooms into a fortress." His eyes found Elias, briefly. "We are not rescued. But we are not doomed, either — not if we work. There are one hundred and four of us on this floor. We have water, the science labs have gas burners, the storage rooms have food from the harvest festival drive. We have two stairwells, both blocked, both guarded. From this moment, this floor is our home, and every person in it has a job.

"If you have medical training, find Ms. Reyes. If you can cook, see Mrs. Petrov. If you are strong, you are on watch rotation. And if you understand electronics —" again, the glance at Elias — "we will need radios, we will need light, we will need to know if anyone out there is still broadcasting. That is not a small job. That may be the most important job on this floor."

He looked around at them all, at the tear-streaked faces and shaking hands.

"We stay together. We stay quiet. We stay alive. That is the whole of the plan, and it is enough. Does anyone object?"

Nobody did. Somewhere below them, faint through the concrete, the chattering went on — patient, endless, hungry. But up here, a hundred people breathed, and moved, and began, in the smallest and most human ways, to organize.

Elias knelt beside the generator socket in the science annex, soldering iron in hand, and started building them a voice.

---

*End of Part One.*

# Comparative Analysis of the Cloud Shared Responsibility Model (CSRM) and the Cloud Center of Excellence (CCoE) in the Context of Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC)

## 1. Introduction

The migration of enterprise IT to public cloud platforms has fundamentally altered how organizations govern their information assets. In legacy on-premises environments, a single organization held end-to-end custody of hardware, networks, applications, and data. In the cloud, operational control is divided between an external Cloud Service Provider (CSP) and the enterprise customer, creating new challenges for governance, risk management, and compliance (GRC).

Two frameworks have emerged as central to addressing this challenge:

- **The Cloud Shared Responsibility Model (CSRM)** — a provider-defined, contractually grounded framework that delineates which security and operational duties belong to the CSP and which remain with the customer across service models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS). It answers the question: *"Who is responsible for what?"*
- **The Cloud Center of Excellence (CCoE)** — an internal, cross-functional organizational construct that establishes cloud standards, policies, and enablement mechanisms so that the organization actually fulfills its side of that division of responsibility. It answers the question: *"How does the organization govern its share?"*

The essential distinction is that **CSRM is an external boundary imposed by the provider, while the CCoE is an internal capability constructed by the organization**. One defines the division of duties; the other operationalizes the customer's half of that division. This paper reviews the literature on both frameworks, analyzes two case studies, compares their approaches to governance, risk, and compliance, and offers recommendations for organizations adopting them.

## 2. Literature Review

### 2.1 The Cloud Shared Responsibility Model

The CSRM is rooted in the NIST definition of cloud computing (Mell & Grance, 2011), which identifies the essential characteristics and service models that make shared responsibility necessary. AWS articulates the canonical formulation: the provider is responsible for **"security *of* the cloud"** — physical data centers, hardware, the virtualization/hosting layer, and managed service operations — while the customer is responsible for **"security *in* the cloud"** — guest operating systems, applications, identity and access management (IAM), data encryption, and network configuration (AWS, n.d.).

The allocation shifts with the service model:

| Responsibility | IaaS | PaaS | SaaS |
|---|---|---|---|
| Data, classification, access governance | Customer | Customer | Customer |
| Applications and configurations | Customer | Shared | Provider (largely) |
| Operating systems, middleware, patching | Customer | Provider | Provider |
| Virtualization, physical infrastructure, facilities | Provider | Provider | Provider |

In every model, data governance and identity management remain with the customer — a point of recurring practical importance.

Two themes recur in critical literature. First, industry analyses consistently attribute the majority of cloud security failures to **customer-side misconfiguration** rather than provider failure; Gartner, for example, projected that through 2025, 99% of cloud security failures will be the customer's fault. Second, providers themselves have recognized that the classic model leaves customers unprepared: Google Cloud's "shared fate" model and AWS's subsequent guidance and tooling extend the CSRM with provider-side support for secure configuration. Regulators and agencies such as ENISA further emphasize that while *responsibility* is shared, *accountability* for data protection is **not** — under frameworks such as GDPR, the customer remains accountable even where the CSP bears operational responsibility.

### 2.2 The Cloud Center of Excellence

The CCoE concept derives from cloud adoption frameworks — most comprehensively Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework (CAF) — and Gartner's research on cloud governance. A CCoE is typically a cross-functional team combining cloud architecture, security, finance (FinOps), and, in mature forms, legal and risk expertise. Its documented functions include:

1. **Strategy and standardization** — cloud usage policies, landing zones, and reference architectures aligned to business objectives and risk tolerance.
2. **Governance and compliance** — compliance validation, risk assessments, audits, and enforcement mechanisms such as Azure Policy, AWS Config rules, and policy-as-code embedded in CI/CD pipelines.
3. **Enablement** — training, pattern libraries, and self-service platforms that make the compliant path the easiest path.

A notable trend in the literature is the shift from purely centralized CCoEs toward **federated governance**: the central team defines policy and guardrails, while execution and innovation remain distributed to product teams. A poorly designed CCoE can otherwise become a bottleneck — the "Department of No" — recreating the slow, gate-based governance the cloud was adopted to escape.

## 3. Case Study Analysis

### 3.1 Case Study 1: Capital One (2019) — CSRM Failure Without Operational Governance

In July 2019, an attacker exploited a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in a misconfigured ModSecurity web application firewall running on an AWS EC2 instance. The SSRF allowed the attacker to query the AWS Instance Metadata Service (IMDSv1) and obtain credentials for an over-privileged IAM role attached to the instance. Using those credentials, the attacker listed and read S3 buckets, exfiltrating data on roughly 100 million individuals, including approximately 140,000 Social Security numbers. The OCC ultimately levied an $80 million penalty against Capital One, and the incident drove significant class-action litigation.

**CSRM analysis:** AWS's share of the responsibility — physical security, the hypervisor, VPC isolation — was not implicated. Every failure sat on the customer side of the boundary: an unpatched application-layer vulnerability, unrestricted access to the metadata endpoint (a problem later mitigated by IMDSv2's token-based requirement), and an IAM role violating least privilege.

**GRC analysis:** The case demonstrates that the CSRM is *descriptive, not prescriptive*. It tells the customer *what* they must secure, but provides no mechanism to ensure they actually do. The root causes — skills gaps, absence of automated configuration validation, and lack of centralized governance over internet-facing deployments — are precisely the failure modes a functioning CCoE is designed to prevent: encoding IAM and network guardrails as policy, continuously auditing privilege assignments, and training teams on customer-side obligations. Notably, Capital One was an early, aggressive cloud adopter; the lesson is that cloud maturity without governance *enforcement* is insufficient.

### 3.2 Case Study 2: Netflix — "Guardrails over Gates"

Netflix operates one of the largest AWS deployments in the world, deploying thousands of changes daily through autonomous engineering teams. Rather than central review boards, Netflix's central cloud and security teams function as an operational CCoE built on the philosophy of **"guardrails over gates"**:

- **Automated baseline enforcement:** Netflix open-sourced tools such as *Security Monkey*, which continuously scanned cloud APIs for exposed ports, permissive S3 bucket policies, and credential drift, alerting on or remediating violations.
- **Golden-path platforms:** Pre-instrumented deployment pipelines (notably via Spinnaker, which Netflix originated) mean that services inherit compliant network topologies, secret management, and least-privilege IAM mappings by default.
- **Resilience engineering:** Chaos engineering tools (Chaos Monkey and related Simian Army tools) actively validate that customer-tier high-availability and failure-recovery configurations work in practice, rather than relying on the provider's availability-zone guarantees.

**Effectiveness evaluation:** Netflix demonstrates a CCoE that operationalizes the CSRM by *converting customer-side obligations into software*. Instead of expecting every developer to internalize AWS's responsibility matrix, the platform team bakes encryption, IAM isolation, network hardening, and monitoring into the default deployment path — making secure CSRM adherence the path of least resistance. Governance scales with engineering velocity rather than against it.

**Caveat:** Public case-study material (engineering blogs, conference talks) is less rigorous than academic literature, and Netflix's tooling has evolved; the case should be treated as an illustrative model rather than a verified outcome study.

### 3.3 Synthesis of the Cases

The two cases are mirror images. Capital One shows that understanding CSRM boundaries provides no protection when the organization lacks mechanisms to *enforce* its half of the model. Netflix shows that when a CCoE translates customer-side CSRM obligations into automated, default-on controls, security and velocity can coexist at scale.

## 4. Comparative Analysis

| Dimension | CSRM | CCoE |
|---|---|---|
| **Origin** | Provider-defined, contractual | Organization-defined, internal |
| **Nature** | Descriptive boundary; largely static per service model | Dynamic; evolves with organizational maturity |
| **Governance role** | Defines *what* must be governed and by whom | Defines *how* governance operates |
| **Risk role** | Clarifies risk ownership | Assesses, mitigates, monitors, and remediates risk |
| **Compliance role** | Provides provider-side attestations (e.g., SOC 2, ISO 27001) | Ensures customer-side compliance posture; maps obligations to regulations |
| **Primary weakness** | Assumes customer execution capacity; misinterpretation drives most incidents | Resource-intensive; can become a bottleneck or silo |

**Strengths of CSRM:** clarity, industry standardization, contractual defensibility, and provider compliance certifications that customers can inherit for their own audits.

**Limitations of CSRM:** it is static and service-model dependent; it does not prescribe implementation; it excludes organizational factors such as skills and culture; and the boundary blurs for newer abstractions (serverless, containers, managed AI services), creating gray zones that customers often misread.

**Strengths of CCoE:** it contextualizes the CSRM for the organization's specific workloads and regulators; it enables proactive, automated governance (policy-as-code, CSPM tooling); it drives training and cultural maturity; and it keeps pace with rapid changes in provider services and responsibility models.

**Limitations of CCoE:** it requires dedicated headcount and executive sponsorship; it risks becoming a centralized bottleneck that developers route around; and its effectiveness varies widely with team capability.

**Synthesis:** The frameworks are complementary halves of cloud GRC. CSRM without a CCoE is a map with no driver — Capital One's lesson. A CCoE without CSRM grounding risks governing the wrong things. Together they form a closed loop: CSRM defines obligations → the CCoE encodes them as guardrails, training, and audits → audit findings and provider model changes feed back into both.

## 5. Conclusion and Recommendations

**Key findings:**

1. The CSRM is necessary but insufficient: it allocates responsibility but does not ensure fulfillment, and most cloud security failures arise from customer-side misconfiguration.
2. The CCoE is the primary organizational mechanism for operationalizing the customer side of the CSRM — most effectively when it acts as a platform-engineering function ("guardrails over gates") rather than a review board.
3. Responsibility is shared, but **accountability is not**: regulators hold the customer accountable regardless of the provider's share.
4. Both frameworks are evolving — providers toward "shared fate" support, organizations toward federated governance.

**Recommendations for adopting organizations:**

1. **Maintain a living responsibility matrix per cloud service used**, not a generic per-provider one — the boundary differs service by service.
2. **Codify CSRM obligations as automated guardrails** using AWS Config, Azure Policy, or Open Policy Agent, so compliant configurations are the default.
3. **Establish a CCoE early in the cloud journey**, starting lean and federating governance as teams mature.
4. **Invest in continuous training** so all stakeholders understand their role in the shared model — the highest-return, lowest-cost control.
5. **Map customer-side CSRM duties to specific regulatory obligations** (GDPR, PCI DSS, SOX, sector rules), since compliance cannot be inherited from the provider.
6. **Assign explicit ownership for tracking CSP service changes**, including updates to responsibility models and provider tooling.
7. **Audit continuously, not annually**, and feed findings back into policy and training.

In the cloud, security and compliance are not the provider's job alone — they are a shared journey, and the CCoE is how an organization drives its half of it.

# Supervillain Creation Project

## Step 1 – Mythological Creature / Basis
**The Gorgon** (Greek mythology — Medusa). A modern version: her "petrifying gaze" is not magic but a psychological gift — she freezes people with fear, shame, and manipulation.

## Step 2 – Basics
- **Name:** Cassandra "Cassie" Gaze
- **Age group:** Late 20s (28)
- **Physical appearance:** Strikingly pale, with sharp, intelligent features and intense, unblinking green eyes that unsettle everyone. Dark hair in a severe bob; she wears minimalist, well-tailored black clothing and moves with a quiet, deliberate stillness.

## Step 3 – Context
**Stillwater**, a seemingly idyllic coastal town famous for its art galleries and wellness retreats. Beneath the calm surface lies a ruthless social scene where reputation is everything and vulnerability is a weakness.

## Step 4 – Childhood (traumatic event and reasons for anger)
As a child, Cassie was a sensitive, gifted artist. Her father, a celebrated local sculptor, stole her sketches for the installation that made him famous. When she told her mother, she was accused of lying. That betrayal taught her that her voice meant nothing — and that the people who should protect you will exploit your gifts. Her anger grew from years of being silenced while her father received the applause that belonged to her.

## Step 5 – Personality (human qualities)
Highly intelligent, perceptive, and articulate, with a sharp dark wit. She is patient and calculating rather than violent, and she genuinely believes she is a vigilante exposing the hypocrisy of Stillwater's elite. Deep down, the artist in her survives — but her canvas is now fear itself.

## Step 6 – Flaws (what makes her an antagonist)
She has lost all empathy for anyone she sees as part of the "corrupt system." She uses people's deepest insecurities to publicly humiliate them, calling it justice. She cannot see the collateral damage: to her, victims are symbols, not individuals. Her need for control, born from a powerless childhood, has become an obsession.

## Step 7 – Entourage
- **a) Sidekick:** *Echo*, a brilliant young hacker, himself a victim of Stillwater's elite. He amplifies her attacks online, making her seem omnipresent.
- **b) Nemesis:** *Detective Elias Vance*, a methodical, empathetic detective. He is her opposite: where she uses trauma to destroy, he uses it to understand. He is the only one who sees the pattern behind the town's "accidental" scandals.
- **c) Significant other:** *Dr. Leo Chen*, a kind psychiatrist who runs a wellness retreat. He sees the vulnerable artist Cassie once was. He is her anchor to humanity — and her greatest weakness.

## Step 8 – Critical moment
**Her origin story:** the night she takes her first revenge on her father, destroying him publicly and choosing to become the Gorgon.

## Step 9 – In-class writing (120–150 words, past tenses)

Cassandra stared at the glistening bronze sculpture — her father's "masterpiece." Years before, she had sketched that design as a lonely, hopeful girl. He had stolen it, and everyone had applauded him. That evening, at his grand gallery opening, she decided to act. While the crowd was admiring his work, she whispered a painful truth into the ear of his biggest investor: his financial ruin. Then she told an art critic about her father's plagiarism. A wave of panic spread through the room. As his world crumbled, her father finally turned and saw her. She met his terrified gaze, unblinking. For the first time in her life, he truly saw her — and he froze, like stone. She felt nothing. That night, the artist died, and the Gorgon was born.

*(~145 words — past simple: stared, decided, whispered; past continuous: was admiring; past perfect: had sketched, had stolen.)*
